The distinction matters because comparing how well settings explain data does not automatically assign probabilities to those settings. Our seed example makes the comparison visible with only one unknown parameter. It is a teaching model, not a reproduction of Fisher's data.

naive-bayes.title: Classifying Without a Table for Every Combination

sources.title: McCallum and Nigam: A Comparison of Event Models for Naive Bayes Text Classification (1998)

blocks: Text classification made the combination problem particularly visible: a vocabulary can contain thousands of word features, and possible documents cannot be exhaustively tabulated. McCallum and Nigam's 1998 comparison examined different event models for naive Bayes, including binary word occurrence and word counts.

That paper did not invent Bayes' rule or every naive Bayes model. It demonstrated why the way we represent observations matters even within this apparently simple family. We will use invented binary sensor signs, then distinguish that model from counting repeated words.

support-vector-machines.title: Separating Examples That Do Not Cooperate
blocks: A separator that makes no training mistakes may still sit unnecessarily close to observations. Maximum-margin methods made the distance from a boundary part of the fitting problem. Real datasets then posed another difficulty: measurement error and overlapping classes can make perfect separation impossible.

Cortes and Vapnik's 1995 support-vector networks paper allowed the classifier to handle data that could not be separated perfectly. A point could violate the margin, but doing so carried a cost. The model could then balance a wider margin against those violations. We will use small geometric examples to understand that choice; the paper's experiments concerned optical character recognition.

hierarchical-clustering.title: Keeping the Smaller Groups Inside the Larger Ones

sources.title: Ward: Hierarchical Grouping to Optimize an Objective Function (1963)

blocks: Grouping many observations poses a practical search problem: there are too many possible partitions to inspect exhaustively. Ward's 1963 procedure described forming a hierarchy through successive merges chosen by an objective. It made the sequence of grouping decisions part of the result.

Once groups contain several sensors, there is more than one way to decide which groups are closest. Ward's criterion chooses the merge with the smallest increase in within-group squared variation. We will begin with single linkage instead: find the nearest pair with one sensor in each group. That lets us point to the distance responsible for each merge. These criteria can produce different hierarchies.

density-based-clustering.title: Finding Shapes Without Supplying Their Centres

sources.title: Ester, Kriegel, Sander and Xu: DBSCAN (1996)

blocks: Spatial databases contained clusters with shapes that centre-based partitions did not describe well, together with observations that should be treated as noise. Ester and colleagues introduced DBSCAN in 1996 to address arbitrary-shaped clusters through a density-based definition.

Its local question is whether a neighbourhood contains enough observations. Connected regions of sufficiently dense neighbourhoods form clusters. Our workshop rebuilds that neighbourhood test, then the lesson follows how those local decisions grow into groups. The plotted sensors are invented.

images-as-arrays.title: Making a Picture Available to a Numerical Machine
blocks: In 1957, Russell Kirsch and colleagues at the US National Bureau of Standards produced a digital scan of a photograph. A picture had to become a collection of numerical samples before their computer could process it. The problem was representation before recognition.

Our tiny tray image follows that same requirement, although it is invented and uses modern array conventions. Giving each measurement a row and column lets us select a region, compare neighbours, or apply the same operation across the picture.

image-thresholding.title: Finding a Cutoff Without Inspecting Every Pixel

sources.title: OpenCV: Image Thresholding, including Otsu's method
Otsu: A Threshold Selection Method from Gray-Level Histograms (1979)

blocks: Thresholding already offered a way to separate image regions, but choosing the cutoff by hand was another problem. Otsu's 1979 method chose a threshold from the intensity histogram by comparing the variation within the resulting groups. It was a method for selecting a threshold, not the invention of thresholding itself.

The useful intuition is to seek two reasonably compact intensity groups. That works only when intensity is a suitable way to separate the objects we care about. Shadows or similar foreground and background intensities can defeat a single global cutoff.

morphology.title: Measuring Shapes in Mineral Images

sources.title: Matheron and Serra: The Birth of Mathematical Morphology

blocks: Matheron and Serra's account traces mathematical morphology to their work in 1964 on the structure of mineral samples. Knowing the amount of a material was not enough; its spatial distribution and sizes mattered. They investigated how chosen shapes could probe the structures in an image.

The shape used to probe an image is a structuring element, also called a footprint. Its geometry determines what an operation considers small, connected, or wide enough. Our seed mask is an invented example of that idea, not a claim that one footprint can distinguish all noise from all objects.

connected-components.title: Following Regions Through a Digital Picture

sources.title: Rosenfeld and Pfaltz: Sequential Operations in Digital Picture Processing (1966), NASA record

blocks: Rosenfeld and Pfaltz's 1966 work addressed sequential operations on digital pictures, including the organisation of picture regions. A computer needs explicit local relationships where a person might simply see a connected shape.

Modern connected-component routines expose the same essential choice: which neighbouring positions may connect? We will use a simple flood fill so every step is visible. It illustrates the task, rather than reproducing the historical paper's algorithm.

image-augmentation.title: Showing a Model Variations of Its Training Examples

sources.title: Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (2012)

blocks: The 2012 AlexNet paper used transformations including crops and horizontal reflections to expand the appearances shown during training. The network had many parameters, and presenting only a fixed view of each training photograph made overfitting a serious concern. This was an influential use of augmentation, not its invention.

The reasoning is that some changes to a photograph should leave its target answer intact. We use that prior knowledge to create additional training views. Our small grid example makes the label-preservation requirement visible before any network is fitted.

transfer-learning.title: Testing Which Learned Features Transfer

sources.title: Yosinski et al.: How Transferable Are Features in Deep Neural Networks? (2014)
PyTorch: Transfer Learning for Computer Vision

blocks: Training a deep model for each new task can require more labelled examples than we have. Yosinski and colleagues studied transfer between image tasks in 2014, examining the difference between more general early features and more task-specific later features. Their results also showed that transfer depends on the relationship between tasks.

That work investigated transfer rather than inventing the general idea of reusing learned knowledge. For our purposes, it suggests a practical question: do the available features already separate our new classes, or does the representation itself need to change?

bounding-boxes.title: Comparing Where Systems Said an Object Was

sources.title: PASCAL VOC 2005: Detection Task and Evaluation

blocks: The PASCAL VOC challenge, beginning in 2005, distinguished recognising an object's presence from predicting its location. The detection task supplied labelled bounding boxes and evaluated predicted boxes through their overlap with the annotations. Shared data and evaluation rules made systems easier to compare.

That challenge did not invent rectangles or overlap. It illustrates why detection needs a localisation criterion in addition to a class score. We will use continuous rectangle boundaries; always check a dataset's coordinate convention before applying the same arithmetic to its annotations.

non-maximum-suppression.title: Making Duplicate Detections Count as Errors

sources.title: PASCAL VOC 2005: Detection Task and Evaluation

blocks: The PASCAL VOC 2005 detection rules counted repeated detections of one object as false detections after the first match. Reporting many plausible rectangles was therefore different from finding many objects. Systems needed a way to resolve competing candidates.

Greedy non-maximum suppression is one commonly used procedure for that job. This example connects the method to a documented evaluation problem without claiming that the VOC challenge invented it. The procedure makes a local decision about overlaps; it does not establish the true number of objects.

forecasting-baselines.title: Giving a Forecast a Reference to Beat

sources.title: Hyndman and Athanasopoulos: The Forecaster's Toolbox

blocks: Forecasters had practical ways to predict before fitting an elaborate model: repeat the most recent observation, or reuse the value from the corresponding season. These rules gave later methods something concrete to improve on.

The forecasting competitions reported by Makridakis and Hibon, including M3 in 2000, compared methods on shared future observations and included simple benchmarks. Some simple procedures competed well with more elaborate ones. We will start with persistence, predicting the next demand from the latest observed demand, and ask whether a later model improves on it over the same future days.

lagged-features.title: Turning Delayed Effects Into Predictors
blocks: A record unfolding through time contains information in its order. Using an earlier reading as a predictor requires preserving which observation was earlier, rather than handing a learning algorithm an unordered collection.

Yule’s 1927 study of disturbed periodic series, including sunspot records, modelled a value through earlier values of the series. This helped develop the autoregressive approach: the record’s own past supplies explanatory inputs. Our demand table uses that idea in a small supervised-learning layout. Every row must be constructed using values available before its target, and a useful lag is not proof that the earlier value caused the later one.

seasonality-and-differencing.title: Describing Changes When Levels Would Not Sit Still
blocks: Time-series modelling developed tools for records whose levels or recurring patterns changed over time. Differencing became a central part of the Box-Jenkins ARIMA approach: model changes when a more stable relationship can be expressed there.

Let's try differencing on a record where we know the trend and repeating cycle we put into it. We can watch what each subtraction removes. A real record may retain changing behaviour afterwards, so differencing is something to inspect, not an automatic guarantee of stationarity.

exponential-smoothing.title: Maintaining a Level Estimate as Observations Arrive
blocks: Exponential smoothing emerged in forecasting work in the 1950s, including contributions associated with Brown and Holt. Forecasters needed practical updates for changing records, rather than repeatedly treating every old observation equally.

Simple exponential smoothing maintains a level. More elaborate versions add trend and seasonal states. We begin with the level-only update so its response to a new observation is visible before adding those components.

autoregressive-forecasting.title: Predicting a Record From Earlier Values of Itself

sources.title: Yule: On a Method of Investigating Periodicities in Disturbed Series (1927)

blocks: Yule's 1927 work investigated disturbed periodic series by relating a value to earlier values of the same process. That gives us a way to learn how earlier readings contribute, while leaving a remainder for variation the relationship does not explain. We will use that idea with Botie's demand history.

Later ARIMA methods combined autoregressive terms with other components, including differencing. Our exercise fits a small autoregression directly with least squares; it is not an automatic ARIMA-selection procedure.

rolling-forecast-validation.title: Replaying Earlier Forecast Origins

sources.title: Hyndman and Athanasopoulos: The Forecaster's Toolbox
Tashman: Out-of-Sample Tests of Forecasting Accuracy (2000)

blocks: Forecasting researchers needed evaluations that respected the order in which observations became available. Tashman's 2000 review discussed out-of-sample testing choices, including rolling origins, rather than treating one fitted historical curve as evidence of future accuracy.

Let's replay the decision at several earlier dates. At each date we expose only the observations that would have been available then, fit the procedure, and record its forecast before checking the later result. The small arrays let us inspect these time boundaries directly.

exploration-and-bandits.title: Experiments Whose Choices Affect What We Learn

sources.title: Robbins: Some Aspects of the Sequential Design of Experiments (1952)

blocks: Robbins's 1952 work on sequential experimental design helped formalise problems in which the next experiment depends on what earlier experiments revealed. Sampling a treatment gathers information, but the chosen treatment also determines the outcome received during that trial.

A multi-armed bandit isolates this exploration problem. Our schedules and numerical rewards are invented. Real watering changes future soil conditions, so the independent-trial bandit is only an initial simplification.

states-actions-and-transitions.title: Planning With a State That Changes After Each Choice

sources.title: Bellman: The Theory of Dynamic Programming (1954)
Stanford CS234: Tabular Decision Processes and Learning

blocks: Dynamic programming developed a way to solve multistage decisions by describing the current situation and the remaining problem. Bellman's work in the 1950s made this recursive view central to sequential planning.

A Markov decision process supplies states, actions, transitions, and rewards. Our dry-or-moist greenhouse is a deliberately simplified model. Its value is that every transition can be inspected, not that two labels fully describe soil behaviour.

discounted-returns.title: Connecting Immediate Feedback to Later Outcomes

sources.title: Sutton: Learning to Predict by the Methods of Temporal Differences (1988)
Stanford CS234: Tabular Decision Processes and Learning

blocks: Sequential prediction needed to account for outcomes that arrive after several intermediate steps. Sutton's 1988 work developed temporal-difference learning, where later predictions help improve earlier predictions before a final outcome is available.

Before using that update, we need to define the quantity predicted. A discounted return combines future rewards with a stated time convention. Our short watering episode makes the accumulation explicit.

bellman-value-iteration.title: Reusing the Remaining Decision Problem

sources.title: Bellman: The Theory of Dynamic Programming (1954)
Stanford CS234: Tabular Decision Processes and Learning

blocks: Bellman's dynamic-programming approach expressed a multistage problem through an immediate choice and the problem remaining afterward. A state's value summarises that remaining problem, avoiding a separate calculation for every history that reaches it.
Value iteration repeatedly applies an optimality update under a known model. Our finite teaching environment separates this planning calculation from learning an unknown model through interaction.

q-learning.title: Replacing a Known Model With Sampled Transitions
blocks: Watkins and Dayan's 1992 paper analysed Q-learning, a method for learning action values from experience without requiring an explicit transition model. It combines an observed reward with a current estimate of the best available continuation.

This belongs to temporal-difference learning: an estimate is moved toward a target partly built from another estimate. Our tabular examples expose the update, including the important exception when a transition ends the episode.

distributions-and-expectations.title: From Games of Chance to Decisions Under Uncertainty

sources.title: Bayes: An Essay towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances (1763)
Huygens: De Ratiociniis in Ludo Aleae (1657), English translation reprinted at Dartmouth

blocks: Players dividing an unfinished game’s stake needed to value outcomes that had not happened yet. Giving each possible prize equal influence would be unfair when the chances were unequal.

Huygens’s 1657 treatise on games of chance developed calculations for the value of an uncertain opportunity, including outcomes with different numbers of equally likely chances. The calculation combined what could be received with how likely it was. That is the historical question behind an expectation.

Our damaged-sensor table uses the same weighted-average reasoning for a different decision. The expected count describes an average across possibilities; it need not be the number in any particular delivery. We will keep that distinction when deciding how many spares to hold.

parameter-posteriors.title: Learning About a Chance From Its Outcomes

sources.title: Bayes: An Essay towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances (1763)

blocks: Bayes’s essay asked how observations could inform an unknown probability. That reverses the direction of a calculation that starts with a known chance and predicts possible outcomes.

For repeated binary trials, a Beta prior and Bernoulli likelihood give a convenient update: count failures and non-failures separately. This is a particular model with explicit assumptions, not a claim that every uncertain rate follows a Beta distribution.

gaussian-sensor-fusion.title: Following a Quantity Through Noisy Measurements

sources.title: Kalman: A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems (1960)

blocks: Kalman’s 1960 paper recast linear filtering as a recursive estimation problem. An estimate and its uncertainty could be carried forward and corrected as new measurements arrived.

Our thermometers isolate the measurement-combination step. The full Kalman filter also predicts how the state and its uncertainty change over time; averaging simultaneous readings alone is not that complete algorithm.

hidden-state-filtering.title: Combining a State Model With a Measurement Model

sources.title: Rabiner: A Tutorial on Hidden Markov Models (1989)

blocks: Rabiner’s 1989 tutorial explained hidden Markov models and their use in speech recognition. A sound recording gives noisy observations of an underlying sequence, rather than a direct label for each state.

We can use the same forward calculation to track the pump. First the transition model tells us how its condition might have changed. We then ask how likely the alarm is under each possible condition and update their probabilities. Our pump example uses supplied transition and alarm probabilities so we can follow each update by hand.

gaussian-process-regression.title: A Distribution Over Functions

sources.title: Rasmussen and Williams: Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning

blocks: Rasmussen and Williams’s 2006 book develops Gaussian processes as a practical framework for regression and classification. A central idea is to describe relationships between function values using a covariance function rather than choose one fixed finite set of coefficients.

For our greenhouse, nearby locations can share information through their covariance. The kernel and noise assumptions decide how far that influence extends and how strongly a reading should constrain a prediction.

minibatch-gradients.title: Trading an Exact Gradient for a Useful Estimate

sources.title: Dive into Deep Learning: Minibatch Stochastic Gradient Descent
Robbins and Monro: A Stochastic Approximation Method (1951)

blocks: An exact expected response can be unavailable even when another noisy observation is easy to obtain. Robbins and Monro’s 1951 stochastic approximation method addressed that situation by choosing successive experiments and updating an estimate from their responses.

Later stochastic optimisation uses the same broad opportunity in learning: a sampled contribution can guide an update without evaluating the entire population objective. A minibatch averages several such contributions and suits numerical hardware. We will inspect that average for a one-weight model, including what changes when the last batch has fewer observations. The original paper was about noisy root finding, not this particular batch training program.

momentum-updates.title: Keeping Useful Direction Across Steps
blocks: Early iterative optimisation methods could make slow progress when their successive directions kept changing. Throwing away all information from the previous step left each update to respond to the current slope alone.

Polyak’s 1964 work studied ways to accelerate iterative methods using information from earlier iterations. The momentum idea we need is to retain a decaying contribution from the previous direction. A direction that persists can build up; opposing contributions can cancel.

We will keep that stored velocity separate from the weight. The convention here adds the current gradient to beta times the previous velocity, then applies the learning rate when changing the weight. That lets us inspect why the weight can keep moving after the latest gradient changes sign.

adaptive-gradients.title: Remembering Both Direction and Scale

sources.title: Kingma and Ba: Adam (2014 preprint; ICLR 2015)
Duchi, Hazan and Singer: Adaptive Subgradient Methods (2011)

blocks: Adaptive subgradient methods used gradient history to change parameter-specific scales. Kingma and Ba’s Adam combined running first and second moment estimates with a correction for their zero initialisation.
Adam is an update rule, not a substitute for choosing a loss or checking generalisation. Our examples calculate the state explicitly; they do not claim that Adam always outperforms other optimisers.

initialisation-and-gradient-checks.title: Keeping Signals Alive Through Layers

sources.title: Glorot and Bengio: Understanding the Difficulty of Training Deep Feedforward Neural Networks (2010)

blocks: Glorot and Bengio examined why deep feedforward networks were difficult to train, including saturation and how activation and gradient scales changed across layers. Their analysis connected weight initialisation to the number of incoming and outgoing connections.

A finite-difference check addresses a different issue: whether an implemented derivative agrees with the loss. Good initialisation cannot repair a wrong derivative, so our lesson keeps these two checks separate.

training-diagnostics.title: Treating Training Time as a Choice

sources.title: Dive into Deep Learning: Learning Rate Scheduling

blocks: A network can keep improving its training fit after its predictions on new examples have started to deteriorate. Stopping as soon as one validation measurement rises can also be premature when that curve is noisy.

Prechelt’s 1998 work compared explicit early-stopping criteria and the tradeoff between training time and generalisation. It treated the stopping rule as something to investigate, rather than a decision made by casually watching a plot. We will use recorded curves to inspect our own declared rule. Learning-rate scheduling changes the updates; validation-based stopping chooses when to keep a fitted state.

popularity-baselines.title: Giving Recommendations a Reference Point

sources.title: Herlocker and colleagues: Evaluating Collaborative Filtering Recommender Systems (2004)

blocks: As collaborative-filtering algorithms multiplied, researchers were making comparisons that used different tasks and different measures of success. Predicting someone’s rating and choosing a useful short list could reward different systems.

Herlocker and colleagues’ 2004 evaluation study examined those choices and organised the decisions needed for a meaningful comparison. Our popularity list supplies an inexpensive reference before personalisation. It can work without a reader’s history, but it also reflects which guides the service previously displayed and counted. We will inspect that reference before asking whether a personalised procedure improves on it.

content-based-ranking.title: Using the Description of an Item

sources.title: Salton, Wong and Yang: A Vector Space Model for Automatic Indexing (1975)

blocks: Vector-space information retrieval represented documents using shared term coordinates, allowing a query and a document to be compared numerically. This provides a foundation for using item descriptions in retrieval and recommendation.

Our guides use two hand-labelled topic coordinates so the comparison is inspectable. Real systems may use terms or learned embeddings, but the coordinate meaning and similarity assumptions still matter.

collaborative-filtering.title: Sharing Judgements Across Readers

sources.title: GroupLens: An Open Architecture for Collaborative Filtering of Netnews (1994)

blocks: GroupLens explored collaborative filtering for netnews, using readers’ ratings to help predict which articles others would find interesting. Shared judgements supplied information that the article text alone might not capture.
Our small rating table uses the same broad idea, but the workshop is a transparent neighbourhood calculation rather than a recreation of the original service.

recommendation-factorisation.title: Sharing Information Through Latent Factors

sources.title: Koren, Bell and Volinsky: Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems (2009)

blocks: Koren, Bell and Volinsky described matrix-factorisation methods that became prominent in recommender systems, including work associated with the Netflix Prize. Learned low-dimensional factors allowed user and item information to interact.
The coordinates are learned to fit the objective. They should not automatically be labelled with human interests such as humour or difficulty unless additional evidence supports that interpretation.

ranking-evaluation.title: Evaluating the Recommendation Task

sources.title: Herlocker and colleagues: Evaluating Collaborative Filtering Recommender Systems (2004)

blocks: Herlocker and colleagues emphasised that evaluating a recommender involves the user task, data, metrics, and experimental design. A numerical comparison is meaningful only when these choices match the intended use.
Our exercise fixes the candidate set, relevance labels, and list length. That lets us calculate exactly what a metric rewards before drawing conclusions about a live recommendation system.

robust-anomaly-scores.title: Estimating a Reference Despite Contamination

sources.title: Huber: Robust Estimation of a Location Parameter (1964)

blocks: Huber’s work formalised robust estimation under departures from an assumed model. The practical concern is that a few contaminated observations should not determine an entire estimate.
Our median and median-absolute-deviation score is a simple robust teaching example, not Huber’s specific estimator. It lets us inspect how the reference changes when an extreme reading is present.

local-density-anomalies.title: Outliers Relative to Their Surroundings

sources.title: Breunig, Kriegel, Ng and Sander: LOF (2000)

blocks: The LOF paper introduced a degree of outlierness based on local density rather than a single global distance threshold. Its comparison lets regions with different densities provide their own local reference.

Our one-dimensional example avoids distance ties to expose the mechanism. The original neighbourhood definition includes ties at the kth-neighbour distance, which can make a neighbourhood contain more than k points.

isolation-forests.title: Detecting by Isolation Rather Than Density

sources.title: Liu, Ting and Zhou: Isolation Forest

blocks: Liu, Ting and Zhou developed isolation-based anomaly detection, using random partitions to separate observations. The method estimates how easily a point can be isolated without first fitting a full density.

Our first tree has supplied splits so every branch can be followed. The second exercise averages path lengths from several trees. A production forest fits many random trees on subsamples and handles depth limits and unresolved leaves.

reconstruction-alerts.title: Using Reconstruction as Evidence

sources.title: Hinton and Salakhutdinov: Reducing the Dimensionality of Data with Neural Networks (2006)

blocks: Hinton and Salakhutdinov demonstrated learning compact representations with neural networks by reconstructing data. A reconstruction objective teaches what information must survive compression.
Using reconstruction error as an anomaly signal is an additional modelling choice. A network may reconstruct some anomalies well, and a normal condition absent from training may reconstruct poorly.

graph-representations.title: Using Relationships Alongside Measurements

sources.title: Kipf and Welling: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks

blocks: Graph-based learning uses both measurements and the relationships between the things measured. Kipf and Welling’s graph-convolution work provides one influential example of using an adjacency structure to share information between nodes.
Before reaching a learned graph model, we need an unambiguous representation. Our pipe network is an invented example, and an edge records a connection rather than proving a causal effect.

graph-random-walks.title: Ranking Through Linked Structure

sources.title: Page and colleagues: The PageRank Citation Ranking

blocks: PageRank used a random-surfer interpretation to relate the importance of web pages to incoming links from other pages. Teleportation provides a way to leave a local link structure and makes the process less dependent on traps.

Our pipe-network walk first studies ordinary transitions. It is a structural probability calculation, not a physical fluid simulation; actual flow depends on pressures and capacities as well as connectivity.

neighbour-aggregation.title: Learning How to Combine Local Neighbourhoods

sources.title: Hamilton, Ying and Leskovec: Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs

blocks: GraphSAGE learned functions for sampling and aggregating local neighbourhood information, allowing representations to be constructed from node features and neighbourhoods. This differs from storing a separate learned vector for every node identity.

Before adding learned transformations, let's calculate the mean of all a node's neighbours. That smaller operation lets us see exactly which readings reach each node. GraphSAGE also samples neighbours and learns how to combine their information; our first example isolates the gathering step.

graph-convolution.title: A Simple Shared Layer on a Graph

sources.title: Kipf and Welling: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks

blocks: Kipf and Welling proposed a computationally efficient graph-convolution approach for semi-supervised node classification. Their propagation rule combines self-loops, symmetric degree normalisation, learned feature transforms, and nonlinearities.

The construction here reproduces one forward layer with supplied weights. Training would require a loss on labelled nodes and an explicit split protocol; the forward calculation alone has not learned a classifier.

link-prediction.title: Learning Representations That Support Pairwise Questions

sources.title: Kipf and Welling: Variational Graph Auto-Encoders (2016)

blocks: Variational graph auto-encoders combined graph-based representations with a decoder for reconstructing links. An inner-product decoder provides a simple way to turn two node representations into a link score.

Our exercise uses supplied vectors and the same basic dot-product decoder. It does not implement variational training, and its output should not be assumed calibrated merely because a sigmoid lies between zero and one.

confounding-and-comparisons.title: Making the Intervention Question Explicit
blocks: Causal modelling distinguishes observing a choice from intervening to set it. Pearl’s graphical framework makes assumptions about common causes and pathways explicit, allowing us to ask when observational comparisons identify an intervention effect.
Our plant example is invented. Its purpose is to expose why a common cause of treatment and outcome can distort a comparison, not to establish an agricultural recommendation.

randomised-experiments.title: Defining Effects Through Alternative Outcomes

sources.title: Rubin: Estimating Causal Effects of Treatments in Randomized and Nonrandomized Studies (1974)

blocks: Rubin’s 1974 paper described treatment effects using the outcomes a unit would have under different treatments, and considered both randomised and nonrandomised studies. Randomisation supplies a known assignment mechanism for comparing groups.
We observe only the outcome under the assignment actually received. The example therefore estimates an average difference; it cannot reveal both possible outcomes for an individual bed.

causal-adjustment.title: Choosing Variables by Their Causal Role
blocks: Observational researchers could record more variables and still disagree about which ones belonged in a comparison. Adjusting for every available variable could change the question or introduce another bias.

Pearl’s graphical approach, developed in Causality and its 2009 second edition, made the assumed relationships explicit. Its back-door criterion identifies sets of variables that can block particular noncausal paths between a treatment and an outcome under the graph’s assumptions. That gave analysts a reason for an adjustment beyond the fact that a column was available.

We will first trace the common-cause path in Botie’s plant example, then calculate the adjusted comparison. The calculation depends on that causal argument; the table cannot verify the assumptions in its own diagram.

treatment-effects-and-overlap.title: Making Observed Groups Represent a Shared Population

sources.title: Hernán and Robins: Causal Inference: What If
Rubin: Estimating Causal Effects of Treatments in Randomized and Nonrandomized Studies (1974)

blocks: The potential-outcomes framework defines an average effect as a comparison of outcomes under two interventions. Hernán and Robins develop identification and estimation methods, including weighting, while making exchangeability, positivity, and consistency assumptions explicit.
Our supplied propensity scores are part of a teaching model. Estimating them from observations adds uncertainty and model dependence; weighting does not automatically remove unmeasured confounding.

saving-fitted-pipelines.title: The Model Is One Part of the System

sources.title: Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: A model could be accurate in a training program and troublesome to maintain once its inputs and surrounding software changed. Copying its coefficient file preserved only part of the procedure that produced its predictions.

Sculley and colleagues’ 2015 Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems examined these surrounding dependencies, including data and configuration. Their analysis showed why the small block of model code could sit inside a much larger maintenance problem. Our first reproducibility check is correspondingly concrete: reload the fitted preparation and weights together, then ask whether known inputs still produce the same predictions.

prediction-input-contracts.title: Treating Data Expectations as Testable Rules

sources.title: Breck and colleagues: Data Validation for Machine Learning (2019)

blocks: Production teams found that a valid model file could still be fed records with changed fields or unexpected value patterns. Such a pipeline might continue running and quietly damage prediction quality.

Breck and colleagues’ 2019 Data Validation for Machine Learning described a system used within TFX to detect these input anomalies, including differences between training and serving data. Validation became a continuing part of the data pipeline rather than an investigation started only after a model failed.
Our small contract begins with explicit feature names, array shape and finite values. Units and operational meaning need their own declarations; the numerical type cannot supply them.

serving-predictions.title: Reducing Differences Between Training and Serving
blocks: A training program can take time to load a model and inspect intermediate results. A service answering repeated prediction requests needs a controlled path from each incoming record to the correct loaded procedure.

Olston and colleagues’ 2017 TensorFlow-Serving paper described a serving system concerned with model lookup, inference performance and moving updated model versions from training into service. Those responsibilities explain why serving is more than calling a fitted function once.

We will begin at the numerical boundary: prepare one request in the declared feature order and apply the same fitted preparation as training. The browser tests that procedure locally. Network transport and running a real service are separate parts of deployment.

model-versioning.title: Preserving the Dependencies of a Prediction

sources.title: Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: Changing an input dataset or a preparation setting can change a model’s behaviour while its prediction function remains byte-for-byte identical. A code revision alone therefore gives the next operator an incomplete account of what changed.

The 2015 Hidden Technical Debt study by Sculley and colleagues described data dependencies, configuration issues and interactions between model components as sources of maintenance cost. Applying version control to such a system requires deciding which surrounding inputs belong to the versioned procedure. We will make that decision visible in a small immutable manifest, keeping its declared preparation and model state together.

monitoring-and-rollback.title: Testing a System That Keeps Receiving New Data

sources.title: Breck and colleagues: The ML Test Score (2017)

blocks: The ML Test Score organised tests and monitoring for production machine-learning systems, including data, models, infrastructure, and changes between training and serving. This reflects a practical reality: model code can remain unchanged while its operating conditions move.
Our small monitoring examples distinguish a changed input distribution from an observed increase in prediction error. Neither should be mistaken for the other.

project-sensor-investigation.title: From Robust Estimates to an Investigation Procedure

sources.title: Huber: Robust Estimation of a Location Parameter
Breck and colleagues: The ML Test Score
Breck and colleagues: The ML Test Score (2017)

blocks: Huber’s 1964 work examined how to estimate a central location when some observations depart from an assumed normal model. It made resistance to contamination a property to analyse, instead of assuming that every unusual value should determine the reference.

Later production work raised a second question: how should a fitted reference be tested and watched once it is used repeatedly? Breck and colleagues’ 2017 ML Test Score organised concrete testing and monitoring needs for learning systems.

This project brings those concerns together with a simple median-based reference. An alert asks for an inspection; a confirmed fault is evidence from that inspection. We will keep those outcomes separate while choosing and testing the alert rule.

project-demand-forecast.title: Evaluating Predictions at the Time They Could Have Been Made

sources.title: Hyndman and Athanasopoulos: Forecasting Principles and Practice
Tashman: Out-of-sample tests of forecasting accuracy (2000)

blocks: Forecast comparisons could disagree because their test procedures exposed different amounts of past data or evaluated only one unusually easy or difficult period. A good fit to the historical curve did not resolve that problem.

Tashman’s 2000 review examined these choices explicitly, including fixed versus rolling forecast origins and whether coefficients were recalibrated. Repeating the evaluation from several earlier dates let a procedure face more than one historical decision boundary. Our synthetic demand project follows that logic: expose the past available at each date, fit the declared procedure, then check its still-unseen next value.

project-seed-counting.title: Turning Pixel Regions Into Measurable Objects

sources.title: Rosenfeld and Pfaltz: Sequential Operations in Digital Picture Processing (1966)
Rosenfeld and Pfaltz: Sequential Operations in Digital Picture Processing (1966), NASA record

blocks: Early digital-picture programs had to turn local pixel operations into descriptions of complete regions. A threshold could mark foreground positions, but counting those marked positions would count pixels rather than the objects they might depict.

Rosenfeld and Pfaltz’s 1966 work on sequential picture operations addressed the organisation of image regions through local relationships. We will use an explicit four-neighbour flood fill to make one such relationship inspectable. The algorithm groups our invented foreground pixels; deciding whether each group is one seed still depends on separation, lighting and the threshold we chose.

design-from-decisions.title: A Requirement Has to Describe Something People Need

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook: development since 1995

blocks: A maintenance team asks for fewer unexpected breakdowns. A model builder reports a better prediction score. Those statements can both be true while the inspection service remains unusable, perhaps because it asks for more inspections than the team can perform. We need to connect the prediction to the decision it changes.

Large engineering projects had to make this connection between a broad need and independently built components. NASA first published its Systems Engineering Handbook in 1995 to collect methods suited to its projects, then revised it as experience exposed further problems. Its design process begins with stakeholder expectations and develops technical requirements that can be checked. A stakeholder is somebody whose use of, or responsibility for, the system affects what it must accomplish.

For Botie's inspection service, that means identifying the action before choosing the model. We can then test a proposed inspection policy against the team's capacity. Whether the predictions are useful still needs evidence from representative pumps; design reasoning cannot supply missing measurements.

design-without-a-model.title: Learning Needs Something to Improve On

sources.title: Martin Zinkevich: Rules of Machine Learning

blocks: A request to improve inspections does not tell us that a learned model is the next useful component. We might lack reliable fault labels, or a simple temperature rule might already handle the decision adequately. Without a working comparison, a model's score tells us little about what it improved.

Drawing on production work at Google, Martin Zinkevich collected Rules of Machine Learning to describe the engineering problems around a model. Its early guidance recommends establishing metrics and starting without machine learning when suitable data are unavailable. An existing rule can make the service usable while exposing which outcomes need to be recorded. Later, that experience gives a learned method something concrete to improve on.

That is the role of our temperature rule. We will count missed faults beside the inspections it requests, using declared illustrative costs. The question is whether another design makes a useful improvement under the same conditions. A more complicated implementation has to earn its place through that comparison.

design-information-boundaries.title: A Model Inherits Its Data Dependencies

sources.title: Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: Production ML systems often depend on data produced by other systems. Sculley and colleagues described how these dependencies and changes in the surrounding system create maintenance problems that model code alone does not reveal. A field can retain its name while its meaning or availability changes.

Our two-clock example makes one such dependency explicit. Event time describes the measurement; availability time describes when our service could use it. These invented timestamps are a teaching contract, not a guarantee that every database preserves the history needed to reconstruct them.

design-pipeline-capacity.title: Put Numbers Against the Boxes in a Design

sources.title: Google: Non-Abstract Large System Design, SRE Workbook, 2018
Google SRE Workbook: resource estimates in a concrete design

blocks: An architecture diagram can connect image decoding to inference without saying whether either stage can keep up with the cameras. Adding more inference workers will accomplish little if decoding is where the requests are accumulating.

Google's 2018 SRE Workbook described Non-Abstract Large System Design as a response to this gap between a diagram and a running system. The approach drew on experience designing production services. It required turning a workload into approximate resource needs, then revising the proposal when those numbers exposed an impractical assumption. The estimates gave teams something to question before discovering a constraint during deployment.

Our image service follows that reasoning on a small pipeline. We will calculate each stage's ideal capacity and find which stage limits the complete path. Those estimates tell us where to measure next. Contention and scheduling overhead still need a real benchmark.

design-queues-and-bursts.title: Waiting Work Can Become Another Source of Failure

sources.title: Little: A Proof for the Queuing Formula, 1961

blocks: A service can have enough capacity for an average day and still struggle when requests arrive together. Requests that cannot run immediately wait. That waiting work occupies resources and can remain after the arrival burst has ended.

Queueing research gave engineers ways to relate workload to waiting. In 1961, John Little proved a relationship between the average arrival rate, time spent in a system and number of items present, under stated assumptions. Counting requests in flight therefore tells us something about the time users are spending there. A burst that is still building a queue needs its own time-by-time account; a steady average cannot describe every interval.
Google's later account of cascading failures showed how production queues interact with timeouts and retries. A delayed request can provoke more work, which delays the remaining requests further.

Botie's first queue excludes those retries so we can inspect the accumulation itself. We will follow arrivals and completed work through separate intervals rather than replacing the changing workload with one daily average.

design-memory-budget.title: Small Devices Made the Whole Inference Engine Matter
blocks: MCUNet examined neural-network inference on microcontrollers with tight memory and compute limits. Its design combined choices about the network with an inference engine suited to those limits. A useful model had to fit the way the device actually executed it.

Our budget is much simpler. We count parameter storage, an estimated peak activation cost per example, and fixed runtime memory. We are not reproducing MCUNet’s engine or claiming that this linear estimate describes every network.

design-edge-or-cloud.title: Communication Belongs in the Design

sources.title: Satyanarayanan: The Emergence of Edge Computing (2017)

blocks: Satyanarayanan’s discussion of edge computing describes the role of computation close to data sources when latency and bandwidth make distant processing difficult. The location of computation changes how much information has to travel and how long a response takes.

Our inspection example compares a local estimate with a simplified remote path. It does not claim that local computation always wins. A larger remote model may be more useful, and many systems divide work between the device and a server.

design-feasible-tradeoffs.title: A Trade Study Needs Criteria Before a Winner

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook: how the guidance developed

blocks: An accurate model can be too slow for the decision, while the fastest model may miss too many faults. Combining those results into one attractive score before checking the limits can hide a design the maintenance team could never use.

NASA's systems-engineering guidance collected lessons from building systems whose components had competing demands. Across revisions following its 1995 first edition, the handbook developed decision-analysis guidance for comparing alternatives with explicit criteria and assumptions. The contribution we use here is a recorded trade study: state what must hold, compare alternatives against it, and leave the reasons for the choice inspectable.

Begin with the hard limits on Botie's table of model results. Among acceptable designs, a dominated choice is one another candidate matches or improves on every stated objective, with an improvement on at least one. Removing those choices narrows the decision without pretending that accuracy and latency are interchangeable. A person still has to judge the remaining trade-offs.

design-sensitive-assumptions.title: Measurements Need an Account of Their Uncertainty

sources.title: NIST: historical development of measurement-uncertainty guidance
Taylor and Kuyatt: NIST uncertainty guidance, 1993
NIST/SEMATECH: uncertainty budgets and sensitivity coefficients

blocks: A design comparison may look decisive because an uncertain input has been written as one exact number. If that number represents the cost of a missed fault, a plausible alternative value could change which inspection policy we choose.

Measurement laboratories faced a related problem when results carried uncertainty descriptions that were hard to compare. International work produced the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement in 1993, and NIST published guidance for applying a consistent approach. An uncertainty budget records the contributions to an uncertain result. Sensitivity coefficients describe how a change in an input affects the calculated output.

We borrow the question about sensitivity for our decision, rather than claiming to perform a full measurement-uncertainty analysis. Botie will change an uncertain cost while keeping the observed outcomes fixed. The scenarios are declared alternatives. They become a probability distribution or confidence interval only if we have evidence supporting that interpretation.

design-prototype-experiments.title: One Change at a Time Can Miss an Interaction

sources.title: Fisher: The Arrangement of Field Experiments, 1926

blocks: An agricultural treatment can have a different effect under another growing condition. Studying one setting at a time can miss that dependence, or confuse the treatment with ordinary differences between plots. Fisher's 1926 paper on field experiments discussed arranging comparisons so their effects and uncertainty could be investigated deliberately.

Factorial designs develop that idea by including combinations of the settings being tested. If changing the batch size helps only with one parameter format, the combination carries information that isolated trials would miss. This is an interaction: the effect of one choice depends on the other.

Our prototype uses illustrative timing measurements for those combinations. Botie will calculate the difference between effects, then ask which further measurements the result calls for. The contrast describes this supplied table. Replication and a suitable statistical analysis would be needed to judge how confidently it generalises.

design-fallbacks.title: A Busy Service Needs a Defined Reduced Behaviour

sources.title: Google: Site Reliability Engineering and the 2018 workbook

blocks: A model cannot always provide a usable prediction. An input may be missing, or the service may be too busy to finish in time. If the surrounding application assumes success on every request, those failures have no defined destination.

Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, first published in 2016, recorded experience with production services under overload. Its account of reduced responses and admission control addressed a practical failure: attempting every request normally could consume the capacity needed to keep the service running. Deciding what work may be deferred or simplified made the reduced behaviour part of the design.

For our inspection service, an unusable sensor record routes to review. That is a deliberate policy for this example, not a universal fallback. We need to ask who receives the case and whether that route can meet the required response time. Calling something a fallback does not give it unlimited capacity.

design-inspection-review.title: Meeting a Specification and Solving the Problem Need Different Checks

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook: development of the guidance
NASA: Product Realization, verification and validation

blocks: Suppose every component passes its tests, but the maintenance team cannot act on the inspection list in time. We have evidence that the implementation matches its tests. We still need evidence that those tests describe what the team actually needs.

NASA's handbook collected systems-engineering practice from its projects and revised that guidance as further mission experience exposed weaknesses. Product-realisation guidance distinguishes verification against specified requirements from validation against intended use. The distinction keeps a successful component check from silently becoming a claim that the complete system solves the operational problem.

This review brings that question back to Botie's inspection service. We can verify numerical requirements on the supplied records. To validate the service, we would also need representative evidence about faults and the team's actual workload. Passing the fixture is a result we can inspect; fewer real breakdowns is a claim that still needs an operational test.

agent-introduction.title: Giving a Language Model a Way to Check

sources.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models, 2022

blocks: A text-generating model can continue from the information it has already received. Looking something up requires another piece of software to perform the lookup and bring its result back. A language-model agent places the model in a loop where its output can help choose that next operation. The application still decides which proposed operations it can execute.

ReAct, introduced in 2022, studied sequences that combined language-model reasoning with actions and observations from an environment. A lookup could provide evidence for the next step, instead of the model continuing from its original information alone. This was a contribution to language-model agents, not the invention of software agents as a whole. We begin with the request and returned observation so each part of that loop has a visible job.

agent-prompts.title: Examples Became Part of the Request

sources.title: Brown and colleagues: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (2020)

blocks: Adapting a language model to a task once commonly meant collecting labelled examples and updating its parameters. Brown and colleagues investigated a different setting in GPT-3: give the model a task and a small number of demonstrations in its input, then test it without task-specific parameter updates. The examples helped specify the requested behaviour, although success varied across tasks.

That distinction matters here. Writing a prompt changes the input to an existing model; it does not train the model in this lesson. An agent adds software that can let the model select another action after seeing a result. Anthropic’s 2024 engineering article distinguishes this from a workflow whose route is already prescribed in code. We will use that distinction, while remembering that the word agent is used more broadly elsewhere.

agent-structured-outputs.title: Programs Needed a Shared Description of Valid Data

sources.title: Crockford: the JSON interchange format, RFC 4627, July 2006
JSON Schema core draft, January 2013, historical work in progress

blocks: A program receiving another program’s answer needs to find particular fields reliably. JSON provided a compact way to exchange named values across programming languages; Douglas Crockford’s July 2006 RFC 4627 documented that format. Valid JSON alone still leaves the application’s question open: which names must this answer contain, and what values are acceptable?

JSON Schema developed a separate description of those requirements. Its January 2013 draft described a contract for the structure an application expects; the maintained specification and guides now define the current rules. A generated model answer needs the same distinction between readable data and an acceptable record. We will validate the fields first, then separately ask whether its asset identifier refers to a real permitted object.

agent-tool-contracts.title: A Missing Response Does Not Mean a Missing Action

sources.title: AWS Builders’ Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs

blocks: Distributed services faced uncertain outcomes before language models began selecting tools. The AWS Builders’ Library describes using a caller-provided request identifier to recognise a retry and avoid repeating a side effect. It also discusses the case where an identifier is reused with different parameters, which should not silently become the same request.

ReAct studied language-model interactions that interleave reasoning and actions, allowing observations to affect subsequent steps. Once a proposed action reaches a real service, ordinary service guarantees still matter. Our workshop separates a model’s candidate request from the application checks that decide whether it can proceed.

agent-context.title: A Model Could Read Retrieved Material at Answer Time

sources.title: Lewis and colleagues: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (2020)

blocks: A model’s stored parameters are inconvenient for information that changes or needs a source check. Lewis and colleagues’ 2020 retrieval-augmented generation work combined a passage-retrieval component with a model that generates text. Retrieval found material to supply at answer time; generation could use that material alongside what the model had learned during training.

Our maintenance assistant needs that separation because a manual can change without retraining every model that may consult it. This workshop begins after candidate passages have been ranked. It decides which the current request may read and which fit the available input budget. The small list procedure is not the paper’s trained retrieval model; it exposes the permission and capacity decisions around retrieved context.

agent-loops.title: An Observation Could Change the Next Action
blocks: A language model answering from its initial input cannot inspect a tool result that has not arrived yet. ReAct explored sequences that interleave reasoning and actions, letting observations affect the next step. This supplied a concrete way to combine language-based task handling with information gathered during execution.

Our controller is smaller than a full agent implementation. It consumes supplied proposals and results so we can inspect termination behaviour. The workshop does not run a language model or reveal its private reasoning. It shows the operational decisions an application must make around whatever model supplies the proposals.

agent-or-workflow.title: Separating a Predetermined Route from a Model’s Choice

sources.title: Anthropic: How we built our multi-agent research system

blocks: Once language models could call tools, developers could give them control over a sequence of operations. That raised a practical question: which decisions should remain in ordinary application code? Anthropic’s December 2024 engineering article distinguished predefined workflows from systems in which a model chooses its next operations. It described patterns used in applications, rather than claiming to have invented workflows or software agents.

Think about the maintenance desk. Retrieving a known record already has a route. Investigating a poorly described fault may require looking at a result before deciding what to inspect next. Our examples use invented measurements to make that design choice visible. They are not benchmark results for any provider or framework.

agent-pydantic-ai.title: Making a Model Response Fit an Ordinary Python Application
blocks: A useful model response still has to fit into an ordinary Python application. The next function may need a particular record, and a tool may need this request’s permitted manual data. Pydantic AI is a Python framework that organises model calls and tools around those requirements. It lets the application declare expected output fields and provide dependencies such as the records a tool may read.

The Pydantic team’s September 4, 2025 v1 announcement emphasised those software-engineering concerns and a stable interface after months of development. The output can be checked before other code consumes it, while dependency injection gives the tool its application-supplied resources. That term means passing in what the tool needs, rather than making it discover a global source itself. Our citation check still has to establish that the named manual supports the answer; accepted Python structure cannot do that alone.

agent-langchain.title: When Every Application Was Rebuilding the Same Loop

sources.title: LangChain team: first Python release on October 24, 2022

blocks: Developers connecting models to documents and external programs kept rebuilding similar pieces of code. LangChain’s first Python package was released on October 24, 2022 to make those pieces easier to combine. A framework supplied reusable components and ways to connect them, while the application still defined the job those components should perform.

The project changed as agent applications became more common. Its October 2025 v1 release focused the high-level interface on the repeated model/tool loop, using LangGraph underneath. Middleware provides named places where application code can intervene during that loop. For the maintenance desk, that is where a bounded unsuccessful search needs an enforced limit. Asking the model to stop and preventing another tool execution are different mechanisms.

agent-langgraph.title: A Useful Workflow Sometimes Needs to Go Around Again
blocks: A fixed sequence of language-model calls can work until an early step returns insufficient evidence. The application then needs a route back to retrieval, or a pause for a person. LangGraph’s January 2024 introduction described cycles and explicit state machines as a way to control those paths.

For Botie, the state contains the evidence gathered for one maintenance request. A node returns an update, and the application decides how that update changes what was already stored. The workshop builds that merge operation on small invented records before the reference code introduces a paused graph.

agent-human-approval.title: Permission Has to Belong to an Operation

sources.title: Saltzer and Schroeder: The Protection of Information in Computer Systems

blocks: Long before language-model agents, shared computer systems needed to control who could read or change an object. Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 account describes protection mechanisms and distinguishes authentication from authorisation. Their discussion also includes requirements for human judgement before granting access.

An inspection assistant adds generated proposals to that old problem. It still needs a trusted component that grants access to a particular operation. Our approval record is a teaching design for binding a decision to a proposal. It is not a claim that a language model, a checkbox or a checkpoint supplies that authority automatically.

agent-mcp.title: A Common Interface for Data Kept in Different Systems
blocks: Assistants could generate text but often lacked a consistent connection to the systems holding a user’s documents and tools. Anthropic introduced MCP in November 2024 to standardise those integrations. A service can describe its capabilities through one protocol instead of requiring a separate custom interface for every assistant.

Our invented maintenance service uses that idea to expose manual content. Sharing a protocol does not settle whether a server is trustworthy, which technician may read a record, or whether a proposed action needs approval. Those decisions remain in the host application and the service that owns the data.

agent-prompt-injection.title: When Retrieved Text Became Part of the Instruction Problem
blocks: Retrieval and tool use let assistants answer from material their developers had never seen. That also gave outside authors a route into the model’s context. NIST’s 2025 taxonomy distinguishes direct injection through a submitted prompt from indirect injection carried by an external resource. The distinction describes the route into the system, not whether a particular attack succeeds.

NVIDIA’s 2023 NeMo Guardrails paper describes programmable checks around an LLM conversation. These checks made the stages of a conversation explicit enough to apply different policies. Our maintenance example studies one of those boundaries: a proposed action must remain within application-issued grants even if the model or a screening step is mistaken.

agent-authorization.title: Permission Had to Follow the Object Being Accessed
blocks: Shared computers had to keep one user’s programs from freely using another user’s files. Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 paper describes design principles including least privilege, fail-safe defaults and complete mediation. The recurring problem is deciding whether a particular operation on a particular object is allowed.

An agent introduces a new way to propose that operation, but the service still has the same responsibility. In our invented workshop, the model proposes an asset operation while application-owned records establish the caller’s tenant and grants.

agent-data-boundaries.title: Managing Data Meant Following It Beyond the Database
blocks: Keeping a database private does not settle what happens when an application copies its contents to another system. NIST’s January 2020 Privacy Framework organised privacy risk around data processing and the organisations involved in it. That gives us a useful question for an agent: which information leaves each boundary, for what purpose, and under whose controls?

Tools such as Presidio address a narrower part of that problem by identifying and transforming sensitive entities in text and other data. Its documentation explicitly warns that automated detection cannot find every sensitive item. Our workshop begins earlier, with a new record containing only the fields this lookup needs.

agent-output-guardrails.title: A Correct String Can Become an Instruction to Another Program

sources.title: CERT: Malicious HTML Tags Embedded in Client Web Requests, advisory CA-2000-02

blocks: When web applications began building pages from submitted and stored text, the browser could mistake some of that text for instructions. CERT’s 2000 advisory on malicious HTML in generated web responses documented this problem. The author of the text and the web page did not have to be the same person; copying untrusted content into a page could give it the page’s apparent authority.

A language model supplies another source of text to the same consuming browser. The application must choose whether that content is displayed as text or interpreted as markup, and encode it for the chosen context. Structured validation answers a different question about field names and values. Botie’s response therefore needs both a usable record and a safe route into the display, while the correctness of the maintenance advice still needs its own evidence.

agent-retries-and-effects.title: A Lost Reply Was a Problem Before Models Called Tools

sources.title: Amazon Builders’ Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs
Amazon Builders’ Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

blocks: Distributed services have long faced the problem of a request whose effect succeeds while its reply is lost. Amazon’s Builders’ Library describes how client request identifiers let a service recognise repeated intent; its idempotent API article was announced in January 2021. An agent calling a work-order service inherits this same communication problem.

The practical idea is to give the intended inspection a stable identity. A repeated delivery of that operation can then recover its earlier result within the receiving service’s documented contract. Our receipt ledger is a teaching model. It does not implement a distributed transaction or promise that every request eventually succeeds.

agent-resource-budgets.title: An Agent Run Inherits the Resource Problems of a Service

sources.title: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center: Circuit Breaker pattern
Pydantic AI: Usage limits and cancellation
Dijkstra: Cooperating sequential processes, semaphore and bounded-resource mechanisms

blocks: Two concurrent programs can each read that the last resource is available before either records that it has taken it. Dijkstra’s account of cooperating sequential processes developed semaphore operations for coordinating access to shared resources. The important step is treating the check and acquisition as one coordinated operation, so the resource is not promised twice.

An agent run inherits that problem when several calls share its remaining allowance. A model can propose work, but the application must reserve the capacity before starting it. Circuit breakers address a separate failure pattern by temporarily stopping calls to an unhealthy dependency. Our reservation ledger keeps completed spending and still-running work visible, so a limit is enforced by the program rather than left as a request in a prompt.

agent-prompt-examples.title: Showing a Task Inside the Input
blocks: The 2020 GPT-3 paper studied tasks presented through instructions and a small number of demonstrations in the model’s input. In that setting, adapting to the task did not require gradient updates during inference. This made the contents of the prompt part of how the task was specified.

For our maintenance desk, that means we can show a supported answer and a request for clarification side by side. It does not guarantee that a model will infer the intended rule. We still have to test what it does with unfamiliar questions.

agent-tracing.title: Following a Request Across Machines
blocks: A slow response was already difficult to explain when a request crossed several services. Each machine could have a local log without showing which work belonged to the same user request. Google’s 2010 Dapper paper described connecting that work through a trace. Individual spans record particular operations and their timing; relationships between spans show how those operations belong together.

OpenTelemetry supplies shared conventions for recording and carrying that relationship across service boundaries. Botie’s manual lookup and model call can then be examined as parts of the request that caused them. The contribution is the connection between those records, not another total-duration number. Our invented timings let us inspect that connection without treating them as measurements of a deployed assistant.

agent-langfuse.title: The Answer and Its Test Used to Live Apart

sources.title: Langfuse project history: tracing, prompt management and experiments

blocks: After a language-model application ships, its developers need to connect a poor answer with the work that produced it. Ordinary request analytics often missed model-specific questions about quality, cost and changing prompts. Langfuse’s July 19, 2023 launch described open-source product analytics for LLM applications built around those needs.

The project first concentrated on tracing and later added prompt management and dataset experiments. That development connects two records that otherwise drift apart: the actual execution and the judgement of its answer. In the maintenance example, a run identifier lets us return from a suspicious score to the retrieved manual and model output that were judged. Langfuse organises that evidence; the evaluator still has to justify what the score means.

agent-evaluation-datasets.title: Testing an Interaction Instead of One Answer

sources.title: HELM: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (2022)

blocks: Benchmarks built around isolated answers leave out much of an agent’s work. AgentBench evaluated language models acting through interactive environments, making sequences of decisions part of the task. HELM separately emphasised evaluating models across scenarios and multiple metrics rather than reducing capability to one favourable number.

Our maintenance tests borrow that question about behaviour: what did the system do in the environment it was given? The small cases here are invented regression fixtures, not a reproduction of either benchmark and not evidence about a particular model’s capability.

agent-framework-tests.title: A Test Double Gives Us Control Over One Boundary
blocks: Software tests often need to observe a caller’s reaction without depending on a slow or unpredictable service. Test doubles replace that dependency with controlled behaviour. Martin Fowler’s 2007 account distinguished several forms, including stubs that supply prepared answers and mocks that can check expected interactions. This was a testing technique before the dependency was a language model.

Pydantic AI’s TestModel and FunctionModel, and LangChain’s mock-model tests, apply the same idea to agent code. Supply a known response and check what the application does next. That lets us reproduce a malformed proposal or a tool error cheaply. It deliberately leaves the real model out, so it cannot establish how often a provider will produce a useful answer; integration tests and task evaluations answer that later question.

agent-model-judges.title: When Exact Answers Were Too Narrow
blocks: Open-ended assistant answers made evaluation harder because several phrasings could be acceptable. The 2023 MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena study investigated model judges and compared their decisions with human preferences. It also studied problems such as sensitivity to answer position, verbosity and the judge’s own tendencies.

That work gives us a reason to test a judge rather than simply trust its score. Our maintenance task is narrower than a general preference contest: does the answer preserve what this supplied manual requires? A study on conversational preference does not establish reliability on that domain-specific question.

agent-error-analysis.title: An Average Score Cannot Tell Us What to Repair

sources.title: Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with CheckList, 2020

blocks: CheckList, published in 2020, proposed behavioural tests for language systems rather than relying only on aggregate accuracy. Tests could target a capability and probe how behaviour changed when the input changed.

That is useful for our desk because “wrong answer” covers several mechanisms. We can test whether the right manual is retrieved, whether the answer uses it correctly, and whether an approved call reaches the correct service. Each failure gives us a narrower question to investigate.

agent-ablation-experiments.title: Design the Comparison Around the Question
blocks: If several parts change together and the score improves, the result does not tell us which part helped. Experimental design addresses that attribution problem by choosing comparisons around the factor we want to investigate. In agent research, the 2022 ReAct study compared its combined approach with alternatives that omitted reasoning or acting, asking what the combination contributed on its tasks.

An ablation removes or changes a component to examine its contribution. Here we change the demonstration set while retaining the recorded model, tool setup and assessment cases. That comparison asks a narrower question than replacing the whole assistant at once. Repeated runs may still differ, and uncontrolled service changes can still affect the result, so retain the actual configurations and observations with the comparison.

agent-release-checks.title: Make a Repeated Experiment Part of the Change

sources.title: Fowler: Continuous Integration, including the documented 2006 revision

blocks: Teams learned that combining everyone’s code only near the end of a project made failures expensive to untangle. Continuous integration brought changes together frequently and checked them with an automated build and tests. Fowler’s account, including its 2006 revision, explains why that repeated check gives a team earlier feedback about a broken change.

Language-model applications need the same repeatable comparison, but the output can vary between runs. Fixed cases and identified prompt/model configurations make that variation inspectable. Tools such as promptfoo bring evaluations into a command-line or integration job. Our release policy decides in advance which measured failures prevent the next shift, rather than choosing a threshold after seeing which candidate it would favour.

agent-adversarial-evaluations.title: Friendly Test Cases Leave Some Questions Unasked
blocks: Once a model participates in actions and data access, ordinary accuracy examples leave gaps. A test writer needs to deliberately search for ways the application can violate a boundary. NIST’s 2024 Generative AI Profile includes adversarial testing among its measurement activities. It treats testing as part of continuing risk management, rather than a one-time certificate.

Current tools such as promptfoo can generate inputs aimed at a stated policy and apply different attack strategies. Our maintenance example begins with the policy and observed result, so we can understand what such a tool would have to measure. The attempts and outcomes below are invented records, not findings from a live assistant.

agent-incident-response.title: Someone Has to Stop the Effects While Others Investigate

sources.title: Google Site Reliability Workbook: incident response, 2018
Google Site Reliability Workbook: canarying releases, 2018

blocks: Operational incidents often need investigation and coordination at the same time.
