Google’s 2018 Site Reliability Workbook describes agreed incident roles and working records so the people repairing a service are not also left guessing who is coordinating the response. Its canarying guidance limits initial exposure while comparing a candidate with the existing service.

NIST’s 2025 revision of SP 800-61 places preparation, detection, response and recovery within continuing cybersecurity risk management. We will apply those ideas to an agent with queued tool actions. Its action history matters because replacing the model or prompt cannot undo an effect that has already reached another system.

agent-iteration-project.title: Keeping a Repair From Becoming a New Failure
blocks: A repair that answers one new question correctly may still break an older question. CheckList’s 2020 behavioural-testing work made particular capabilities and input changes explicit tests for language systems. A discovered failure could then become a repeatable case, rather than disappear inside the next average score.

Keeping those cases is the basis of this maintenance project. An experiment dataset connects each stored task to its expected behaviour, and a recorded execution shows what a candidate actually did. Langfuse provides tools for organising that comparison, but the task supplies the acceptance rule. We will carry the repaired incident into the next run alongside earlier requirements, so a new success cannot hide an old regression.

agent-guardrail-boundaries.title: Software Needed Boundaries Before It Could Choose Its Own Steps

sources.title: NIST Secure Software Development Framework, February 2022

blocks: Software teams have long needed a way to turn a security concern into a development requirement they can check. NIST’s 2022 SSDF organises practices for preparing development work, protecting software and responding to vulnerabilities. That problem remains when a model writes part of the program or chooses which operation to request.

An agent adds a controller whose proposals depend on text and changing context. We can still describe a forbidden consequence precisely: no record from another tenant may be returned, and no public post may be created without its required authorisation. Those statements give us something more useful to test than whether the agent sounded careful.

agent-guardrail-coding.title: Generated Code Still Has to Survive Independent Review

sources.title: Fagan: Design and code inspections to reduce errors in program development, 1976

blocks: A program can compile and still implement the wrong requirement. Michael Fagan’s 1976 work at IBM described formal inspections of designs and code, with participants given explicit review roles and defects recorded for correction. Reviewing the test plan was part of that process too. The aim was to find mistakes close to where they were introduced rather than wait for a finished system to reveal them.

A coding agent makes proposed patches quickly, and may be able to edit the tests that would reject its own patch. Independent review therefore still needs a fixed statement of the task, evidence about every changed path, and tests whose authority does not come from the generated patch. The workshop asks whether Botie repaired the parser within the agreed scope, even when his own test run is green.

agent-guardrail-sandbox.title: A Process Needed Limits on More Than Its Files

sources.title: Docker: the project’s 2013 introduction and the existing container primitives

blocks: Running someone else’s program creates a practical problem: how can we observe it without letting it freely alter the surrounding machine? Operating-system isolation provides limits on what a process can see and use. Docker’s public introduction in 2013 made existing Linux container mechanisms easier to package and operate; it did not invent the underlying idea of separating processes.

A container still shares important host machinery, and its configuration decides what is exposed. Mounting a host directory as writable can let generated code alter that directory even if the network is disabled. Our profile inspection therefore keeps filesystem access, credentials and execution privileges visible separately. These fixtures review a proposed configuration; actually testing and maintaining isolation remains an operating-system and deployment responsibility.

agent-guardrail-supply-chain.title: A Build Needed a Traceable Origin
blocks: Once software builds consumed many dependencies and ran on separate services, checking the source repository was no longer enough to identify the file being shipped. The file could have been produced from another revision or by a different build process. SLSA was introduced publicly in 2021 to organise progressively stronger software-supply-chain controls, including a record of how an artifact was produced.

That production record is provenance. A verifier needs to establish who issued it and which artifact it describes, under a stated trust policy. Botie’s green test report should therefore name the same candidate revision and artifact waiting for release. Even authentic provenance does not establish that the source is bug-free; it lets us connect the checks to the actual output we are deciding whether to publish.

agent-guardrail-mcp-trust.title: A Shared Tool Interface Made Discovery Useful

sources.title: Anthropic: Introducing the Model Context Protocol, November 2024

blocks: Assistants needed access to information held in many systems, and each custom connector repeated some of the same integration work. Anthropic introduced the Model Context Protocol on November 25, 2024 to provide a common way to connect those sources and tools. A server can describe capabilities through that protocol, while a host decides which of them to make available to its application.

Discovering a tool is not the same as reviewing its current behaviour. The 2025-11-25 specification includes descriptions, argument schemas and notifications that the available tool list changed. Those fields can influence a model’s next request, so the host must notice when the reviewed description or schema is no longer the offered one. A familiar short name cannot stand in for that comparison.

agent-guardrail-mcp-auth.title: Delegation Needed a Destination

sources.title: OAuth security best current practice, RFC 9700

blocks: Giving an application a person’s password lets it do far more than one limited job. OAuth developed a different arrangement: issue access authority for a defined purpose instead. RFC 6749 specified OAuth 2.0 in October 2012, separating the resource owner, client and service holding the protected resource. The receiving service still needs to know which authority was intended for it.

Deployment experience exposed credentials accepted in the wrong context. The February 2020 JWT best-practice document, RFC 8725, includes checking the intended audience when JWTs are used, and RFC 9700 records later OAuth security guidance. MCP’s HTTP authorisation builds on those mechanisms. The workshop starts after token validation and asks whether the verified issuer, destination and scope belong to this service; it never treats a readable token as verified authority.

agent-guardrail-application-actions.title: Transaction Review Had to Describe the Actual Transaction
blocks: Approving access has always needed a connection to the thing being accessed. Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 protection paper discussed controls that introduce human judgement before access and mechanisms that check the requested operation. A person’s general willingness to let a program work is different from reviewing a particular change to a particular record.

Transaction-authorisation guidance makes that distinction concrete: show the actual operation, retain what was approved, and enforce it at execution. Agent frameworks now offer a pause around a proposed tool call, but a resumed conversation cannot establish that the customer, amount or record version stayed unchanged. Botie’s approval must remain attached to the same inspection proposal when the receiving service acts.

agent-guardrail-memory-delegation.title: Saving Context Also Saved Its Trust Problem
blocks: A program can keep notes between steps without changing its model’s weights. That stored context lets later work continue from earlier observations. In the 2023 Generative Agents study, Park and colleagues stored natural-language experiences, formed reflections and retrieved relevant memories to guide later behaviour in a simulated town. The study supplied a concrete architecture for making earlier experience part of a later model input.

Remembering text also preserves whatever was wrong with that text. A summary may carry an outside instruction into another worker’s context while losing its original source label. The maintenance task therefore needs to keep ownership and review information with saved notes. Passing a note to a child worker is also separate from granting that worker tools: remembered prose cannot create the authority to read another customer’s records.

agent-guardrail-release-lab.title: An Evaluation Needed to Observe Actions
blocks: An assistant can say the expected words after performing the wrong action. Evaluating only its final sentence would miss that failure. AgentBench, introduced in 2023, evaluated language models interacting with environments, making a sequence of decisions part of what had to be assessed. That shifted the observation from one answer to what the system did while trying to complete the task.

For this release exercise, we need the operation records as well as the answer. The receiving service tells us whether a write actually occurred, while an application-owned scenario lists the effects that were permitted. Langfuse can organise the runs and their scores, but it cannot supply that permission policy on our behalf. The final test asks whether Botie can finish legitimate work while keeping forbidden effects out of a fresh shift.

software-feature-contracts.title: A Model Can Depend on More Than Its Code

sources.title: Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: A model project can look like a small program wrapped around a learning algorithm. In practice, the learned coefficients also depend on the records that supplied their inputs. Sculley and colleagues’ 2015 technical debt paper examined how those surrounding dependencies make ML systems difficult to maintain. An upstream change can alter the meaning of a prediction even when the model’s source code stays untouched.

Feature order is one particularly small dependency we can inspect. A coefficient learned for temperature must keep receiving temperature when another program sends the record. A schema describes the named fields; an adapter arranges accepted fields into the representation the model expects. This agreement is a software contract. Keeping names attached to values gives us a way to check it before a matrix calculation conceals the mix-up.

software-fitted-state.title: Fit Once, Apply the Same Preparation

sources.title: Buitinck and colleagues: scikit-learn API design, 2013

blocks: Machine-learning libraries needed different algorithms to work together without every caller learning a new interface. The scikit-learn team’s 2013 API-design paper described a common arrangement: fit learns from a dataset, while prediction and transformation methods use the resulting state. That consistency lets a preprocessing object and a predictor participate in the same application.

For a centring procedure, the learned state includes the training mean. Later requests should use that stored reference. Relearning a mean from each request would give the same measurement a different meaning whenever its neighbours change. Separate fit and transform methods make the intended distinction visible, and a changed-batch test checks that the implementation actually respects it.

software-retrieval-shortlists.title: Keeping the Current Best Candidate Close
blocks: Selecting the next best item was an algorithm problem long before a retrieval system had thousands of passages to rank. J. W. J. Williams’ 1964 Heapsort algorithm described a heap: an array organised so an extreme item stays at its root. In his formulation the least item is immediately available, and insertion or extraction repairs the ordering without sorting the entire collection again.

That idea also helps a bounded shortlist. Keep only the best k candidates, with the weakest retained candidate easiest to inspect. A better arrival can replace it. Our workshop uses sorting to show which positions win; the Python challenge builds the bounded heap. Both must preserve passage IDs and the declared tie rule. Efficient selection does not decide whether the retrieval scores identify useful evidence.

software-workflow-dependencies.title: Dependencies Outlive a Single Script

sources.title: Kahn: Topological sorting of large networks, 1962

blocks: A job cannot use an input that another job has not produced yet. Large project networks made that ordering problem important well before ML pipelines. A. B. Kahn’s 1962 paper presented a method for topological sorting: arrange network activities so prerequisites come before the activities that depend on them. A cycle means that no ordering can satisfy all those dependencies.

Workflow systems such as Airflow apply dependency graphs to executable tasks. A directed edge says which task must precede another; an acyclic graph has no route that leads back to itself. For Botie, preparing training data must finish before the job that fits the model. The readiness matrix below isolates that ordering question. A real workflow also needs to identify the actual dataset version and record task failures.

software-named-request-contracts.title: A Named Field Still Needs an Agreement

sources.title: JSON Schema: object properties and required fields
JSON Schema: null is a value
Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: An API, or application programming interface, lets one program ask another to do something. Here a sensor client sends readings to a prediction service. The two programs need an agreement about what those messages mean. Does leaving out temperature ask the service to use a default? Does sending null mean that no reading was available? Without that agreement, a harmless-looking replacement can change the model’s input.

A schema records rules that a program can check, including which field names must be present and which values they may contain. JSON Schema treats presence and null as separate questions. That distinction addresses a practical problem in exchanging records: a sender can produce a readable message that the receiver misunderstands. Sculley and colleagues’ 2015 paper describes how such upstream dependencies become a maintenance problem in ML systems. We will make this small part of the agreement explicit before applying the model’s saved transformations.

software-schema-evolution.title: Two Programs Rarely Upgrade at the Same Instant

sources.title: JSON Schema: object properties and required fields
JSON Schema: dialect and vocabulary declaration
Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: A client is the program making the request; the server is the program handling it. They are often installed or updated separately. That creates the compatibility problem: how can we improve the server while existing clients still depend on yesterday’s messages? A request schema describes the accepted fields and values, but it cannot make all those programs upgrade together.

The ML technical debt paper published in 2015 discusses dependencies and consumers that can be difficult to track. An agent calling a retrieval tool is another such consumer. We will keep two explicitly supported message versions and write a small translator for each. These translators are adapters. They let the rest of the search code receive one agreed record while older callers finish migrating.

software-semantic-contracts.title: An Interface Can Carry the Right Type in the Wrong Unit

sources.title: NASA: Mars Climate Orbiter mishap investigation, PhaseI
Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: Programs have exchanged numerical measurements much longer than they have served learned models. A number can be well formed while using the wrong unit. NASA’s 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter investigation identified a ground-software file that supplied impulse data in English units where the receiving calculations expected metric units. The software interface specified a convention, but the integration failed to enforce it.

Our temperature service has the same kind of disagreement on a smaller scale. The fitted model saved a Celsius reference, and the new sensor supplies Fahrenheit. We need a semantic contract: an agreement about what the values mean, including their units. Checking field names and numerical types comes first, but the model also needs the measurement expressed in the representation it learned.

software-tool-errors.title: A Lost Answer Leaves the Caller Unsure What Happened

sources.title: RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs (2023)

blocks: When one program calls another over a network, performing an action and receiving its answer are separate events. A training service can create a job just before the connection fails. The caller needs a way to describe that uncertainty, because repeating the command may create another job. A sentence written for a person is difficult for a program to use reliably: its wording can change without the failure changing.

HTTP, the request-and-response protocol used by web services, supplies status and method rules. RFC 9457, published in 2023 as a replacement for RFC 7807, adds a standard format for more specific problem details. A stable problem type lets the client recognise the category while the explanatory wording improves. We will use short outcome codes to decide what can happen next, and keep a lost answer separate from a confirmed failure.

software-contract-tests.title: Write What Must Hold Across Many Inputs

sources.title: NumPy: allclose tolerance and broadcasting rules

blocks: A hand-calculated example can tell us what one prediction should be. It cannot list every future request. Some promises are easier to describe as relationships: if the same named measurements arrive in another order, the result should stay the same. Property-based testing starts from such a promise and tries many inputs that could contradict it.

Claessen and Hughes first published QuickCheck in 2000. The tool generated inputs for developer-written properties and helped reduce failures to smaller examples. Hypothesis brings this approach to Python. The useful result is a counterexample: a concrete input that breaks the stated promise. For our model interface, we will begin with the saved-centre mistake, then test whether changing feature order exposes another mistake. Each relationship must follow from the model’s actual behaviour.

data-partition-statistics.title: Move Summaries Instead of Every Row
blocks: Suppose a training dataset is spread across more files than one worker can process quickly. We can give each worker a portion, but then we need a way to combine its answer. Sending every original row back to one machine can recreate the bottleneck we were trying to remove.

Dean and Ghemawat's 2004 MapReduce paper described a programming model that separated work on individual records from combining results with the same key. The system handled distributing that work and retrying failed tasks. It gave programmers a way to describe the calculation without writing a separate scheduling system for every job.

For our mean, each worker can send a sum and a count. Those quantities still tell us how much data its answer represents, even when file sizes differ. A local mean alone has discarded that information. We will follow these small summaries through the same kind of merge, using ordinary Python before needing a distributed service.

data-asof-features.title: Historical Retrieval Needs a Time Boundary

sources.title: Gojek and Google Cloud introduce Feast, January 2019

blocks: A corrected reading can tell us more about yesterday while still being something we did not know yesterday. Database researchers had to represent that distinction long before it became a training-data problem. In their 1986 paper, Snodgrass and Ahn separated when a fact applied in the world from when it was recorded in a database. Keeping both lets us ask what was believed at an earlier time, even after a correction.

Machine-learning teams face a related difficulty when rebuilding inputs for old predictions. Feast, announced by Gojek and Google Cloud in 2019, provided a shared feature store for training and serving. Its historical retrieval selects feature values against each training row's timestamp rather than attaching today's value to every old example.

Our lesson keeps an additional availability timestamp explicitly. A measurement may describe an earlier event but arrive after the prediction. We must check both boundaries to reconstruct what the service could have used. That extra rule is part of this example's contract; a feature store's point-in-time label alone does not promise it.

data-contract-quarantine.title: Checking Data Before Fitting

sources.title: Breck and colleagues: Data Validation for Machine Learning, SysML 2019

blocks: A training program can finish successfully after a producer changes the meaning of a column. There need not be a syntax error or a crash. The model simply learns from the wrong observations, and its predictions may later feed more bad examples into training.

Breck and colleagues described this production problem in their 2019 paper on data validation at Google. Their system, part of TensorFlow Extended, compared incoming data with a schema and examined differences between datasets. A schema records expectations such as which fields exist and which values are allowed. Checking those expectations gives a pipeline a chance to identify a bad input before fitting another model.

We will make the decision visible on one sensor batch. First inspect readings against an allowed interval, then decide whether the rejected fraction requires stopping the batch. The example is small enough to check by hand, but the responsibility is the same: a completed calculation does not establish that its input was suitable.

data-stream-windows.title: Streaming Systems Cannot Wait for an End of File

sources.title: Akidau and colleagues: The Dataflow Model, VLDB 2015

blocks: A file eventually ends. A stream of sensor readings may keep arriving, with yesterday's disconnected sensor sending a reading after today's records. Waiting for every possible late record would prevent us from publishing an answer at all.

The 2015 Dataflow Model paper addressed this tension between timely results and out-of-order data. It separated the time an event happened from the time a system processed it. Windows grouped events into intervals; watermarks estimated how far event time had progressed. Triggers made the decision about when to emit a result explicit. These ideas became part of Apache Beam's processing model.

A watermark is an estimate, so a late reading still needs a policy. We will inspect membership in one event-time window and watch what a delayed record changes. The local exercise exposes that decision; it does not implement Beam's distributed state or recovery.

data-artifact-lineage.title: Track a Run’s Inputs and Outputs
blocks: A model file can outlive the job that created it. When a prediction changes later, the filename alone tells us very little. Which source records were read? Did preparation code change, or did somebody replace a file in place? Answering those questions becomes harder when each pipeline tool records its work differently.

OpenLineage brought projects including Airflow and dbt into a common effort to describe these relationships. Its September 2021 initial release included a shared specification and integrations. The model distinguished a job, which describes work to do, from a run, which is one execution, and identified the datasets involved. That lets information from separate tools describe a connected processing history.

We will start with a much smaller record: the exact dependencies of one prepared feature file. This record is a manifest. Comparing its input and code identities lets us explain why a previous result can be reused, or why replacing an input requires doing the calculation again.

databricks-lazy-dataframes.title: Why a Table Calculation Became a Platform Problem

sources.title: Zaharia and colleagues: reusable distributed data, NSDI 2012

blocks: Training can revisit the same observations many times. On a large collection of machines, repeatedly writing intermediate results out and reading them back adds work that does not improve the model. Spark began as a Berkeley research project in 2009 and was released as open source in 2010. The researchers’ 2012 paper explained how keeping reusable data in distributed memory could help repeated calculations, while recording the operations made lost portions of the data recoverable.

Spark supplies the engine: it can divide work between processes and combine their results. Running that engine for a team creates another job. Someone has to provide compute, connect the approved data and make executions inspectable. Spark’s creators founded Databricks in 2013 to build a company around this kind of shared data work. Databricks is the managed platform; Apache Spark is a separate open-source project that can also run elsewhere.

Our first calculation uses Spark’s table interface. The Spark SQL work published in 2015 described how named columns and declared operations give a query engine information it can use to plan execution. A request for a filtered table describes a result; it need not calculate every row immediately. That is the distinction Botie will build on the workshop floor.

databricks-shuffle-skew.title: Why Matching Records Can Leave One Worker Waiting
blocks: Counting records for one pump across many files requires combining contributions that began in different places. The same issue appears when two tables need to match rows by an identifier. A distributed system must arrange for the matching contributions to meet somewhere; this movement between partitions is called a shuffle.

Spark SQL’s 2015 paper described planning table calculations as operations the engine can optimise and execute across a cluster. The plan still has to respect the grouping we requested. If one pump owns most of the work, sending all of that group to one task can leave the other workers waiting. More machines help only when the work can actually be divided between them.

We will split one pump’s work into temporary partial groups while preserving its original identifier. A count can later add those partial counts. Spark may already perform local aggregation or choose an adaptive plan, so the workshop exposes a routing decision we can reason about rather than predicting a real cluster’s task counts.

databricks-delta-snapshots.title: How Could Readers Agree While Files Were Changing?

sources.title: Delta batch reads and time travel

blocks: A training job may read a collection of files while another job is replacing part of that collection. Seeing only half of an update can produce a dataset that no writer intended to publish. The problem is deciding which files belong together as one complete table state.

Delta Lake puts a transaction log alongside the data files. A successful commit records which files form the next table version. A reader can use one committed version even while later work creates another. Databricks released Delta Lake as an open-source project on April 24, 2019; the 2020 research paper explained the design for reliable analytical tables over object storage.

Spark performs the table calculation. Delta Lake supplies the versioned table storage that this read relies on. On the floor we keep full local snapshots so you can see exactly which records a version selects. The real format uses its log and retained files to reconstruct that state.

databricks-replay-safe-ingest.title: Why Finding a File Was Not the Same as Finishing It
blocks: As cloud storage filled with incoming files, repeatedly listing every directory became an expensive way to discover the next input. Teams also had to remember which discoveries had actually reached their output after failures and retries.

Databricks announced Auto Loader in public preview in February 2020 to handle incremental discovery and loading of files from cloud storage. It is a file source used with Spark streaming, with checkpointed progress so a restarted query can continue. A checkpoint is the durable recovery record for that query; it has to work with the destination’s commit behaviour.

That distinction is what we will build. A discovery says there is a file to consider. A completed-file record says its effect belongs in the committed output. Keeping the output rows and progress together prevents a lost acknowledgement from becoming a second copy of the observations.

databricks-change-data-capture.title: Keeping a Copy Current When the Source Keeps Changing
blocks: Once a source table can correct or delete a reading, copying it once is no longer enough. A downstream training table needs to learn which records changed and what happened to them. Change data capture, usually shortened to CDC, is the process of communicating those inserts, updates and deletions.

The Delta Lake work described in the 2020 paper addressed dependable table updates over analytical files. Delta’s MERGE operation can match incoming rows to stored rows and apply declared insert or update rules. That gives us somewhere to express a correction, but we must still decide which source change is authoritative when messages arrive out of order.

Here the source gives each pump’s changes an increasing sequence. A later arrival can therefore be recognised as an older change. We also keep the version of a deletion behind the consumer’s view, so an old update cannot make a deleted pump reappear.

databricks-lakeflow-quality.title: A Pipeline Needed More Than a Working Query
blocks: A query can produce the right table once and still leave a team with a difficult daily job. Its input tables must be ready, failed attempts must be recoverable, and a bad reading needs a declared consequence. Those responsibilities used to be scattered around the transformation code.

Databricks announced Delta Live Tables in May 2021 to let authors declare datasets, their dependencies and quality expectations together. The pipeline system could inspect those definitions and manage their updates. The current interface used here is Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines. Delta Lake remains the versioned storage underneath; a pipeline is the process that builds and refreshes datasets.

An expectation is a named condition that a row should satisfy. It still needs a policy: keep and report the failing row, exclude it, or stop this update. We will keep the condition and its consequence visible as separate components, then inspect the actual rows training receives.

databricks-mlflow-lineage.title: Which Experiment Produced This Model?
blocks: After several training attempts, a folder of model files and a list of scores are hard to interpret. Which settings changed? Which input version did each model see? Can a colleague repeat the run that produced the good result? A useful record has to keep the model file attached to the procedure and evidence that produced it.

Databricks introduced MLflow as an open-source project on June 5, 2018. Its announcement described the difficulty of tracking experiments and reproducing them across different machine-learning tools. MLflow Tracking groups a training attempt’s settings and results under a run ID. Code can log those details through its programming interface, and a person can compare the runs on a screen. It also keeps output files, such as the trained model, with the run that produced them.

A managed MLflow service is available in Databricks, and the open-source software can also be used elsewhere. In this lesson we use the tracking idea: keep a complete record for each attempt, then compare only attempts measured against the same validation evidence. Recording a score makes it inspectable; choosing a fair comparison is still our responsibility.

databricks-unity-catalog-access.title: A Shared Table Needed a Shared Access Decision

sources.title: Unity Catalog history and open-source announcement, June 2024

blocks: As teams used the same data from different workspaces and tools, finding a table and deciding who could read it became connected problems. Separate catalogs and access settings could disagree. A job that found a useful training table still needed an enforceable answer about whether its actual identity was allowed to use it.

Databricks introduced Unity Catalog in 2021 as a shared governance system. The managed service now covers data and AI objects. Databricks announced an open-source Unity Catalog project in June 2024. The managed Databricks service and the open-source project are related products with different operational scope; the SQL reference here uses the managed service’s documented privileges.

A catalog records what objects are called and where they belong. Access rules attach privileges to those objects and to principals, the users, groups or service identities receiving permission. We will follow one training job through those relationships, so a successful read in somebody else’s notebook cannot stand in for the job’s own permission check.

databricks-historical-features.title: Reusing a Feature Without Rewriting Its Past

sources.title: Uber Engineering: Michelangelo and its shared feature store, September 2017

blocks: A feature is an input a model reads. Temperature is one simple feature in our example. When several models need the same input, rebuilding it separately can give training and live prediction different definitions. A feature store keeps reusable feature data and metadata so those consumers can request a shared input.

Uber’s September 2017 account of its Michelangelo platform described a shared feature store for training and prediction. It is an influential published example of the need to reuse inputs consistently, rather than a claim that one company invented every part of feature storage. Databricks’ feature engineering interfaces address related work through reusable tables and model-linked lookups.

Reusing a definition still leaves a time question. A prediction made before a correction was published could not have read that correction. Databricks documents point-in-time feature lookup for matching each prediction to its earlier eligible feature rows. Delta time travel chooses a table snapshot; this lookup chooses a row for each prediction within that retained history.

systems-inference-batching.title: Batching Trades Waiting for Shared Computation
blocks: Training software often processes several examples together because a processor can share work across them. An online service receives requests one at a time, and the first person in a group must wait while the others arrive. The batch that makes good use of the hardware can still give that person a slow answer.

The Clipper system, presented in 2017, treated prediction serving as a separate problem from training. Its adaptive batching adjusted how many queued requests a model processed together while respecting a latency objective. The useful change was to make batch size depend on the model's observed performance rather than assuming a larger batch was always better. Current servers such as Triton also expose controls for queue delay and batching.

Our first example follows requests already assigned to one batch. We will distinguish time waiting in the queue from time spent computing. A later scheduler has to make its decision using both, because sharing computation cannot recover time a request has already spent waiting.

systems-agent-deadlines.title: A Deadline Follows the Request

sources.title: gRPC and Deadlines, Google SRE guidance, February 2018

blocks: A service can call another service, which calls a third. If each starts a fresh timeout, the complete request may take much longer than its caller agreed to wait. Work can also continue consuming resources after the caller has given up.

In a 2018 gRPC article, Google site reliability engineer Gráinne Sheerin explained why clients should set deadlines deliberately. gRPC is a framework for calling procedures in another process across a network. Its deadline support lets the caller put a time boundary on that work, and implementations can propagate the remaining allowance to downstream calls. The allowance shrinks as work happens; another service does not receive a fresh budget simply because it started later.

An agent making several tool calls has the same dependency. We will calculate what remains before starting the next call. Cancelling a request still requires cooperation from the work it started, especially if an external action may already have happened.

systems-kv-cache-memory.title: Reusing Attention State Consumes Memory
blocks: A language model generates a response one token at a time. Earlier tokens still matter to later ones. Saving the intermediate arrays called attention keys and values avoids calculating them again at every generation step, but the saved state grows as conversations grow. Fitting the model's weights in memory does not establish that all those conversations will fit too.

Kwon and colleagues studied this serving problem in their 2023 PagedAttention paper. Requests had different, changing cache sizes, so reserving large contiguous regions could leave memory unused inside or between allocations. Their design borrowed paging ideas from operating systems: manage attention state in smaller blocks and keep a record of which blocks hold each sequence. The vLLM serving system used that arrangement to support more useful work within its memory budget.

Before comparing ways to reserve memory, we need to count the values a conversation actually requires. This lesson calculates the storage for those arrays first. A real server also has bookkeeping overhead and temporary arrays, so its measured memory will exceed this deliberately isolated quantity.

systems-context-cache.title: A Cache Entry Needs a Reuse Contract
blocks: Reusing an earlier response can save a network request and the work behind it. Web caches also exposed the uncomfortable question: when is the earlier answer still an answer to this request? A page can change, and the same address can produce different responses for different callers.

The 1999 HTTP/1.1 specification documented rules for caching, including freshness and matching the request to the stored response. Later specifications refined those rules; RFC 9111 brought the caching specification forward in 2022. A cache key identifies a possible match, while reuse rules decide whether that match may actually be served. An address by itself cannot settle both questions.

An agent response has further dependencies, such as retrieved evidence and model configuration. We will identify those dependencies before deciding whether an old answer is reusable. This is an application-level contract. HTTP headers alone cannot decide whether the current user may see a previously generated answer.

serving-prefill-decode.title: Why Generating an Answer Changed the Serving Problem

sources.title: vLLM: serving metrics and their definitions

blocks: Once a model has learned its parameters, using it to produce an output is called inference. A service has to arrange that work for the people sending requests. Putting several requests through a model together can use the hardware more efficiently. That arrangement is a batch. Generating text complicates it: the model produces a token, uses that growing text as context, and returns to produce another. One answer may finish while its neighbour still has a page to write.

In 2022, the Orca research serving system addressed batches that stayed fixed for an entire response. Its iteration-level scheduling reconsidered the participating requests after each generation step. That gave finished requests a way out and waiting requests a way in. We will return to that decision later. First, we need to see where a reader waits. The invented timestamps below explain timing measurements used by serving systems such as vLLM; they are not measurements of either implementation.

serving-prefix-reuse.title: The Same Beginning Was Being Calculated Again
blocks: An attention layer calculates arrays called keys and values for the tokens it has processed. Later tokens use those arrays when attending to the earlier context. Keeping them avoids recalculating the entire earlier sequence for every generated token. This saved working information is the key/value cache, usually shortened to KV cache. Its memory grows as requests retain more tokens.

The 2023 PagedAttention work addressed how to manage that growing memory without requiring one large continuous allocation for each sequence. It used smaller blocks. vLLM is a language-model serving system; its prefix-caching design also lets compatible requests reuse blocks for an unchanged beginning. A prefix is that beginning, up to the first changed token. Our workshop makes this decision visible with token lists and an explicit compatibility check. The runtime’s full memory manager is outside this example.

serving-continuous-admission.title: Why a Batch Should Not Wait for Its Longest Answer
blocks: Batching several requests can make a model’s hardware do more useful work at once. A fixed batch becomes awkward when the requests need different numbers of output tokens. A short answer finishes, but the longest answer is still being generated. If the membership of the batch cannot change, another request waits outside while that place is unused.

Orca’s 2022 iteration-level scheduling addressed this problem by choosing the participating requests again between generation steps. This is the idea behind the changing batch we will build. A real runtime must also decide how much work and memory each step can accept. Our smaller model admits requests in queue order and reserves their full token allowance, so we can inspect those two decisions without implementing a serving engine.

serving-cancellation-pressure.title: A Stop Message Has to Reach the Running Work
blocks: When the interface and the worker run in different processes, closing a result on the screen does not directly stop the computation. The worker needs a way to learn that the caller no longer wants it. Systems that make remote calls have long needed this distinction. gRPC is one such system: its cancellation message communicates that a call is no longer wanted, while the application handling that call remains responsible for stopping its work.

That separation matters for generated answers because the worker may still own cache memory while it stops. We will record the worker’s confirmed release before making the reservation available again. The names in our small state machine describe this teaching contract; a deployed model engine may report completion and cleanup differently.

serving-canary-effects.title: Trying a New Service Before Sending Everyone to It
blocks: A new service version can pass tests and still behave differently under real traffic. Gradual deployment lets a limited share of requests use the new version while the rest keep using the established one. That trial version is often called a canary. Kubernetes documents this approach for services; the same deployment question arises when the version being changed is a model. The selected users receive real candidate responses.

Another approach copies requests to a comparison service while returning only the primary service’s answer. This is traffic mirroring, also called shadowing. Envoy’s routing documentation describes a mirror response that stays off the primary response path. Hiding that response does not stop the copied request from calling another service. Our booking example follows this consequence: deciding which answer to display cannot also serve as permission to create a booking.

robot-perception-frames.title: Geometry Connects Separate Sensors

sources.title: Denavit and Hartenberg: A Kinematic Notation for Lower-Pair Mechanisms Based on Matrices, 1955
Dellaert and Hutchinson: robotics perception geometry

blocks: An arm joint describes motion relative to another joint. A camera describes an object relative to the camera. Giving both descriptions numbers does not make their origins and directions agree. Mechanical systems needed a consistent way to connect these local descriptions before a learned detector entered the picture.

Denavit and Hartenberg's 1955 paper described mechanisms using matrix relationships. Writing each relationship explicitly made it possible to combine a chain of links through matrix algebra. The useful idea here is a change of coordinates: the object stays where it is while we express its position using another origin and set of axes.

We will use a supplied rotation and translation to turn a detector's position into the robot's coordinates. This known rigid transform is simpler than estimating calibration or the robot's location. It lets us inspect the geometric step between recognising an object and choosing where the robot should move.

robot-observation-latency.title: State Estimation Connects Measurements Across Time

sources.title: Kalman: A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems, 1960

blocks: A sensor reports where something was when the measurement was taken. The object can keep moving while an image is transferred and a detector processes it. Treating the answer as a measurement of the present position mixes two different times.

Kalman's 1960 work on filtering and prediction described a changing system through its state and a rule for how that state evolves. The estimator could carry its prediction forward and combine it with observations, accounting for uncertainty. That made the interval between observations part of the model rather than an unmentioned gap.

We will begin with the prediction part alone. A conveyor moves at a supplied constant velocity, so Botie can advance an old position by the time that has passed. This is a short-interval teaching approximation. It does not estimate unknown velocity or perform the full Kalman measurement correction introduced later.

robot-feedback-corrections.title: Feedback Uses the Result of the Last Action
blocks: A steam engine's speed changes when its load changes. A governor responds to that speed and adjusts the steam supply, so the next action depends on what the machine is actually doing. This is feedback: measure the result and use it to change the input.

Maxwell's 1868 paper On Governors examined why such regulators could settle or develop oscillations. Feeding a measurement back into a machine creates a changing loop, so a correction that points in the right direction can still be poorly timed or too strong. The loop's behaviour needs analysis of its own.

Our robot uses a much smaller proportional rule. A larger position error asks for a larger correction, and a new measurement informs the next move. A learned detector may provide that measurement; its static accuracy alone does not establish the stability of the resulting controller.

robot-actuator-windup.title: Integral Action Needs to Know About Saturation

sources.title: Åström and Rundqwist: Integrator Windup and How to Avoid It, 1989

blocks: Integral control remembers error over time. That memory helps a controller remove a persistent offset, but an actuator has a physical limit. If the motor is already at maximum output, accumulating more error cannot make it push harder. The stored correction can keep demanding too much even after the target is close.

Åström and Rundqwist's 1989 paper examined this windup problem and methods for avoiding it. Their account also noted that the issue had appeared in earlier controller designs and returned with digital implementations. Back-calculation uses the difference between the requested command and the command the actuator could apply to correct the integral state.

We will inspect one discrete update with an explicit actuator limit. Botie can then remember what the mechanism actually did, rather than assuming every requested action happened. The exercise isolates a proportional-integral controller; adding a learned perception model does not remove the actuator's limits.

state-predict-correct.title: How Do We Estimate Something We Cannot Measure Exactly?

sources.title: Kalman, 1960: a recursive filtering and prediction method
Dellaert and Hutchinson: localisation and Bayes filtering

blocks: A moving system presents two imperfect sources of information. A motion calculation tells us where an object should have gone; a sensor gives a noisy reading of where it is. Replacing the estimate with every reading follows the sensor’s noise. Ignoring the readings lets errors in the motion calculation accumulate. The estimation problem is to use both, while accounting for how uncertain each one is.

Kalman’s 1960 paper gave a recursive solution for a linear filtering problem: carry a current estimate and its error covariance forward, then revise them when a new measurement arrives. The error covariance describes how uncertain the estimated coordinates are and how their errors are related. Recursive means the next step uses the previous result instead of recalculating the entire observation history. The Kalman filter is this predict-and-correct procedure under its stated model assumptions. We will first work with one conveyor position and known expected movement, so the role of each quantity is visible before extending to matrices.

state-missing-observations.title: The Estimate Has to Continue Between Observations

sources.title: Kalman, 1960: a recursive filtering and prediction method
Barfoot: State Estimation for Robotics, author’s text

blocks: Separating prediction from measurement correction made recursive filtering useful for more than one stream of perfectly timed readings. Between observations, a system still moves. The earlier estimate and the motion model let us predict its next state, including the uncertainty added by that movement. A new sensor reading supplies a separate correction when it is available.

The Kalman formulation introduced in the previous lesson keeps these operations distinct. We use that separation when a camera frame supplies no position: perform the prediction and leave out the measurement correction. Barfoot’s treatment of state estimation develops the broader motion and observation models behind this reasoning. Our chronological example handles an absent reading; using a late reading from an earlier time requires another decision.

state-gating-association.title: Which Observation Belongs to the Object We Were Following?

sources.title: Neira and Tardós, 2001: joint compatibility in stochastic mapping
Barfoot: State Estimation for Robotics, author’s text

blocks: Tracking adds a question that a detector alone does not answer. A detector reports objects in the current image; the tracker needs to know which report continues an earlier object’s history. Assigning observations to those continuing objects is called data association. An assignment can look plausible by position and still attach the history to the wrong object.

In robotic mapping, Neira and Tardós examined a related problem in 2001: matches that each look plausible alone can be incompatible when considered together. Their joint-compatibility method considered that combined evidence. We will use a much smaller one-track example. First reject readings that disagree too much with the predicted position and uncertainty. If several still fit, our rule leaves the identity unresolved instead of claiming to have solved the full assignment problem.

state-model-uncertainty.title: What Happens When the Filter’s Error Assumptions Are Wrong?

sources.title: Welch and Bishop: Kalman filtering and assumed noise statistics
Barfoot: State Estimation for Robotics, author’s text

blocks: The Kalman filter’s correction depends on how much error its model expects from movement and from observation. That raises a practical problem: those error statistics have to come from somewhere. If we understate motion error, a prediction can retain too much influence even while new readings keep disagreeing with it. A small reported variance then describes the assumptions we supplied, rather than demonstrating that they were right.

Welch and Bishop’s introduction works through the effect of changing assumed noise statistics in a concrete Kalman-filter example. Barfoot develops state estimation with those modelling questions in view. We will examine a conveyor whose simulated movement departs from its predictor, then compare the result with an independent reference. The reference helps test the estimate; it must stay out of the estimate’s own input.

security-retrieval-authority.title: Authorisation Is a Service Responsibility
blocks: Shared computers had to let several people use one system without giving everyone access to everyone else’s files. Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 account of information protection described principles such as checking each access and granting only the authority needed for the job. Authentication establishes who is asking; authorisation decides whether that requester may perform this operation on this object.

A retrieval model supplies another fact: which passage seems relevant. It supplies no permission to disclose the passage. The service must check the user’s access even when the model ranks a protected record first. OWASP’s current guidance carries the same deny-by-default and per-request checks into web applications. Our deliberately high-scoring forbidden passage tests that separation.

security-private-aggregates.title: A Privacy Claim Needs a Neighbouring-Dataset Definition

sources.title: Dwork and colleagues: Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis, 2006

blocks: Publishing a statistic can reveal something about a person even after their name is removed. Researchers studying statistical databases therefore needed a privacy claim about what changes when one person’s information changes. Dwork, McSherry, Nissim and Smith’s 2006 work connected the random noise used in a release to the sensitivity of its calculation: the greatest effect one allowed contribution can have.

Differential privacy concerns the behaviour of the randomised release across those neighbouring datasets. The neighbouring-dataset definition matters before we choose noise. Here the participant count is fixed and public, and one person has one bounded value that may be replaced. We will calculate the mean’s resulting influence bound. The exact teaching mean is still an exact disclosure; bounding it alone does not make it a private release.

security-model-artifacts.title: Object Reconstruction Can Execute Behaviour

sources.title: Van Rossum and Peters: PEP 307, including unpickling security, 2003

blocks: Python programmers wanted to save an object and reconstruct it later, including the state its class needed. Pickle saves those objects. Rebuilding an object is more powerful than reading a list of numbers: reconstruction can invoke Python behaviour. A saved preprocessing object therefore brings a different loading question from a plain table of coefficients.

The 2003 PEP 307 proposal extended the pickle protocol and explicitly rejected earlier checks that had suggested untrusted unpickling could be made safe. Its warning was to avoid loading pickles from untrusted or unauthenticated sources. That history matters when a model file arrives as an apparently passive download. We will check its bytes against an independently trusted expectation before loading anything; a matching digest still leaves the choice and constraints of the loader to be reviewed.

security-training-provenance.title: The Training Set Is an Input Someone Can Change

sources.title: Biggio, Nelson and Laskov: Poisoning Attacks against Support Vector Machines (2012)

blocks: A learned model changes when its training evidence changes. That gives someone who can supply examples a way to influence later decisions without editing the model’s code. Deliberately manipulating that learning material is called poisoning. The material might be a labelled example or a proposed model update; the important question is what the contributor can actually change.

Biggio, Nelson and Laskov studied this problem for support vector machines in 2012. They constructed training examples to increase later test error, examining how a learner could be influenced through its data supply. Our smaller workshop uses the average of accepted targets so the effect of each record is visible. Before fitting it, we will decide which sources and reviewed labels this release is allowed to use, and keep the accepted record identities with the result.

security-backdoor-evaluation.title: Ordinary Validation Can Miss Conditional Behaviour
blocks: Reusing a pretrained model or asking someone else to train it saves work, but also means receiving behaviour we did not build ourselves. Ordinary validation checks the examples we chose. It can miss a hidden rule that responds to another condition. A deliberately introduced rule activated by a particular input pattern is a model backdoor; the activating pattern is its trigger.

The 2017 BadNets paper investigated outsourced training and demonstrated networks that performed well on ordinary validation examples while misbehaving on attacker-chosen inputs. This made the training and model supply path part of the investigation. Our workshop supplies original and changed predictions for reviewed image pairs. We will measure the observed conditional failure, without assuming that a bad result alone proves who trained the model or how that behaviour arose.

security-adversarial-threat-models.title: Small Chosen Changes Could Cross a Learned Boundary

sources.title: Szegedy and colleagues: Intriguing properties of neural networks (2013)

blocks: Ordinary sensor noise is not usually chosen to make a particular model fail. An opponent may choose its input for exactly that reason. An adversarial example is an input deliberately selected or changed to cause an unwanted model result under stated constraints. This is a prediction-time problem: the model may already be trained, and the opponent works through the inputs it receives.

Szegedy and colleagues reported in 2013 that carefully selected small image changes could cause neural-network misclassification, and that some changes transferred between models in their experiments. Their results raised a different question from average accuracy on collected images: what can a chosen nearby input make the model do? We use a visible two-input threshold model to examine that question. The permitted coordinates and change size are explicit assumptions, not evidence about what a real person could alter in a sensor.

security-prediction-api-controls.title: What Can Repeated Questions Reveal About a Model?

sources.title: Tramèr and colleagues: Stealing Machine Learning Models via Prediction APIs (2016)

blocks: A prediction API lets another program send inputs to a model kept on a server and receive its answers. The owner can offer useful predictions without distributing the model files. Repeated answers still reveal how the model behaves, though. Model extraction tries to use that query access to build another model with similar behaviour; recovering the original source code or exact weights is not required.

Tramèr and colleagues demonstrated extraction through prediction services in 2016, including methods for several model families. They also found that removing confidence scores alone did not eliminate harmful extraction. Our workshop examines controls around the service: count the evaluated rows inside a batch, and return the output the public task actually needs. These decisions limit work and exposed detail, while the useful answers still reveal something about the model.

simulation-time-steps.title: Approximate a Changing State by Following Its Rate

sources.title: Euler Archive: Institutionum calculi integralis, volume 1, 1768

blocks: A physical model may tell us how quickly a state is changing without giving us a convenient formula for its value later. Before a computer could draw a simulated trajectory, numerical methods gave people a way to approximate one from local changes. Euler's 1768 integral-calculus volume is part of that development.

The step rule named for Euler starts with the current state and its current rate of change. It uses that rate to estimate the change over a chosen interval, then repeats from the new estimate. This makes a changing process calculable in separate steps, but it also assumes the initial rate is adequate for each whole step.

That assumption is what Botie will test. An oversized step can make a cooling process oscillate even when the continuous model settles smoothly. Modern libraries offer several solvers because accuracy and stability depend on the problem and the step rule. We start with explicit Euler so the source of the error is visible.

simulation-paired-trials.title: Simulation Is an Experiment with a Random Input

sources.title: Glasserman and Yao: Some Guidelines and Guarantees for Common Random Numbers, 1992

blocks: Suppose we test two dispatch policies in simulation. One receives a quiet shift while the other receives a rush of difficult orders. Their different costs now include the different conditions, making the policy change harder to judge. Simulation researchers used shared random inputs to compare alternatives under related conditions.

Glasserman and Yao examined this established technique in their 1992 paper on common random numbers. Their analysis asked when sharing randomness actually improves a comparison. The benefit comes from how the paired outcomes move together; merely reusing a seed is not a guarantee of a better estimate.

Our exercise makes the pairing explicit by giving both policies the same simulated shift. We compare their costs within that shift before combining evidence across shifts. A reproducible generator helps create the scenarios, but matching the conditions that matter is the experimental design decision.

simulation-system-identification.title: Learning Can Begin with a Physical Model

sources.title: Åström and Bohlin: Numerical Identification of Linear Dynamic Systems from Normal Operating Records, 1966
Robotics and Perception: learning motion models

blocks: An engineer may know the form of a machine's motion without knowing its coefficients accurately. A motor's response can differ from its nominal specification, and a controller built around the wrong response will make poor predictions. Measuring inputs beside the resulting outputs gives us evidence about the missing parameters.

Åström and Bohlin's 1966 work on identifying linear dynamic systems studied learning such models from operating records. System identification is this task of estimating a system's behaviour from observations. It connects a chosen physical model with statistical estimation instead of requiring every coefficient to be supplied in advance.

We will estimate just one gain through the origin using least squares. The model says which relationship to fit; the recorded observations determine its coefficient. An offset or a delay would change the model we need, so a good fit to this restricted example cannot establish that every physical effect has been captured.

simulation-transfer-checks.title: Variation Can Help a Model Cross the Reality Gap
blocks: A visual model can learn the lighting or textures of a simulator so well that it struggles with real images. Making the simulator look realistic in one particular setting does not tell us which details the model is relying on.

Tobin and colleagues' 2017 domain-randomization work varied rendering conditions while training a model for robotic object localisation. By seeing many appearances, the model had less reason to depend on one simulated appearance. The researchers studied whether that training could transfer to real images. This was an experimental response to the gap between simulated and real observations, not a guarantee that arbitrary variation would solve it.

Botie's policy-cost table applies the broader comparison idea to a smaller problem. We will change the supplied conditions and see whether a policy still behaves acceptably. The original paper studied visual transfer; our table does not reproduce that experiment or establish safety in an unseen physical setting.

numerical-stable-normalisation.title: Why a Correct Formula Can Lose Its Answer

sources.title: David Goldberg: What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic

blocks: Scientific software has long had to calculate with measurements far larger or smaller than everyday whole numbers. A finite computer representation must round values and limit their range. A useful final answer can therefore be lost in an intermediate operation that the format cannot store.

David Goldberg’s 1991 survey explained these practical problems for people building computer systems. It connected floating-point representation and rounding rules to failures in real calculations. In our NumPy example, float64 uses a fixed 64-bit format: a finite component can fit while its square exceeds the format’s range. That is overflow.

We only want a direction, so we can change the common scale before squaring. The geometry stays the same, and the products fit in a safer range. We will inspect that change one operation at a time, then test it on a new encoder output.

numerical-identifiable-models.title: A Good Fit Could Still Leave the Parameters Unknown

sources.title: NumPy: least-squares solutions, rank and singular values
Golub and Kahan: singular values and least-squares computation, 1965

blocks: Suppose every calibration test turns two heaters up together. A fitting program can learn their combined heat output while leaving each heater’s contribution unresolved. Repeating that same operating pattern gives it more records of the combined effect, without asking the question that separates the gains.

A least-squares fit chooses coefficients by minimising the sum of squared prediction errors. Computational work on these fits had to address both noisy equations and weakly determined answers. In 1965, Gene Golub and William Kahan described a numerically stable way to calculate singular values and a matrix’s pseudo-inverse, which extends the idea of an inverse to such fitting problems. These calculations can expose changes to the coefficients that the measurements constrain strongly, weakly or not at all.

That historical numerical work does not tell us which heater is stronger. It helps us recognise when a returned coefficient is a convention rather than an independently measured effect. We will first design a setting on which two fitting models disagree, then give the missing information its linear-algebra names.

numerical-gradient-checks.title: Checking the Derivative Against the Running Calculation

sources.title: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams: learning representations by back-propagating errors, 1986

blocks: Training adjusts a model’s weights to reduce a chosen numerical measure of prediction error. We need to know how that measure changes as each weight moves; a derivative describes this local change. As neural networks gained more trainable weights, calculating those derivatives efficiently became essential. Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams’ 1986 paper showed how back-propagating errors could train internal representations. A sign or indexing mistake in that calculation can send later weight updates the wrong way.

Finite differences offer another route for a small check: move an input slightly, evaluate the function again and compare the change. This numerical approach predates modern automatic differentiation. It tests the running function rather than repeating the same derivative code, but its answer depends on the interval and on rounding in the two evaluations.

We will begin with a smoothly changing error measure, called a loss, then give the checker an absolute-error corner. The aim is to understand what a disagreement tells us before treating a neat matching number as proof that the derivative is correct.

numerical-adaptive-steps.title: Spending Calculation Where the Curve Changes

sources.title: SciPy: adaptive initial-value solvers and tolerances

blocks: A simulation estimates a changing state at a sequence of times. Very short fixed intervals can waste calculations while the state barely changes. Long intervals can miss the change a training example was meant to capture. Numerical differential-equation solvers therefore needed a way to assess a proposed advance before accepting it.

One approach compares two approximations for the same future time while sharing some of the intermediate rate calculations. Embedded Runge-Kutta methods are a family that uses this arrangement. Dormand and Prince published one such pair in 1980; SciPy’s RK45 uses that pair to control local error and choose its internal steps.

We will build the idea with the simpler Euler update from the earlier timestep lesson. One full step and two successive half steps give us an inspectable disagreement. That can guide a retry with a shorter interval, while leaving the question of the physical model’s accuracy separate.
